items.narration: Mia gets 2 cookies. Sam gets 2 cookies. Is it fair? Yes or no?
items.why: Mia has 2 and Sam has 2. They have the same, so it is fair.

items.narration: There are 2 apples and 2 friends. Each friend gets the same. How many apples does each get?
items.why: Give one apple to each friend. Then no apples are left. Each friend gets 1.

items.narration: 4 ducks swim to 2 ponds. Each pond gets the same. Hop the frog to how many ducks each pond gets.
items.why: Put one duck in each pond. Then one more each.

items.narration: There are 4 stickers and 4 friends. Each friend gets the same. How many stickers does each get? 1, 2, or 4?
items.why: There is one sticker for each friend. Each friend gets 1 sticker.

items.narration: Sam has 6 cookies. He shares them with 2 friends. How many cookies does each friend get?
items.why: Hand out one cookie at a time to each friend. Each friend ends up with 3.

items.narration: Lily has 6 berries. She shares them with 3 friends. How many berries does each friend get? 2, 3, or 4?
items.why: Give each friend one berry. Then give another to each.

items.narration: Max has 8 toy cars. He shares them with 2 friends. How many cars does each friend get?
items.why: Give each friend one car at a time. Each friend gets 4.

items.narration: 9 grapes are shared by 3 friends. Hop the frog to how many grapes each friend gets.
items.why: Give 3 friends one grape each, three times. Each friend gets 3 grapes.

items.narration: Ana gets 4 cookies. Ben gets 2 cookies. Is it fair? Yes or no?
items.why: Ana has more than Ben. They need the same amount, so it is not fair.

items.narration: There are 10 stars. 2 friends share them equally. How many stars does each friend get?
items.why: Give one star to each friend, again and again. Each friend gets 5.

items.narration: Zoe has 8 pencils. She shares them with 4 friends. How many pencils does each friend get? 1, 2, 3, or 4?
items.why: Give 4 friends one pencil each. That uses 4. Give one more each. Each friend gets 2.

items.narration: There are 9 apples. 3 friends share them equally. How many apples does each friend get?
items.why: Give each friend one apple, three times. All 9 are shared. Each friend gets 3.

items.narration: 10 balloons are shared by 5 friends. Hop the frog to how many balloons each friend gets.
items.why: Give 5 friends one balloon each. Then give one more each. Each friend gets 2.

items.narration: 4 friends each get 2 cookies. All the cookies were shared equally. How many cookies were there?
items.why: Count 2 for each friend. 2 and 2 and 2 and 2 is 8.

items.narration: There are 6 cookies for 2 friends. Which way shares them equally? 4 and 2, 3 and 3, or 5 and 1?
items.why: Equal means the same number each. 3 and 3 is the same, and it makes 6.

items.narration: How many dots are in the ten-frame? Is it 6, 7, or 8?
items.why: Count each dot one by one. There are 7 dots.

items.narration: Count the apples. How many are there? Type the number.
items.why: Count each apple one time. There are 12 apples.

items.narration: Move the frog to fifteen.
items.why: Count up from 0 to 15. Fifteen is five past ten.

items.narration: Which number is twelve? Is it 21, 12, or 2?
items.why: Twelve is one ten and two ones. That is 12.

items.narration: Type the number thirty.
items.why: Thirty is 3 tens and 0 ones. We type 30.

items.narration: Mia has 3 tens and 5 ones. What number is that? Type it.
items.why: 3 tens is 30. Add 5 ones to get 35.

items.narration: How many tens are in the number 42? Is it 2, 4, or 42?
items.why: The first digit tells the tens. In 42, the 4 means 4 tens.

items.narration: Move the frog to twenty-seven.
items.why: Start at 20. Count 7 more to reach 27.

items.narration: Which number is forty-six? Is it 64, 36, 41, or 46?
items.why: Forty is 4 tens. Six is 6 ones. So forty-six is 46.

items.narration: Lena wears player number 24 on her shirt. Does 24 tell how many, or is it a label?
items.why: A player number is a label for the player. It does not count anything.

items.narration: Type the number forty-eight.
items.why: Forty is 4 tens. Eight is 8 ones. Together that is 48.

items.narration: A number has 2 tens and 7 ones. Is it 72, 27, or 29?
items.why: 2 tens is 20. Add 7 ones to make 27.

items.narration: Move the frog to forty-three.
items.why: Start at 40, which is 4 tens. Count 3 more to reach 43.

items.narration: The pizza shop is at house number 35. Does 35 tell how many, or is it a label?
items.why: A house number tells where a house is. It does not count things.

items.narration: Which is the same as thirty-nine? Is it 3 tens and 9 ones, or 9 tens and 3 ones?
items.why: Thirty-nine starts with thirty, so 3 tens. Then 9 ones. That is 39.

items.narration: Count by 1s. 7, 8, 9. What number comes next?
items.why: When you count by 1s, you add 1 each time. 9 and 1 more is 10.

items.narration: Count by 2s. 2, 4, 6. What number comes next? Is it 7, 8, or 9?
items.why: When you count by 2s, you add 2 each time. 6 and 2 more is 8.

items.narration: Count by 10s. Hop the frog from 0 to 30.
items.why: Hop by 10s. 10, 20, 30. That is three hops.

items.narration: Count by 5s. 5, 10, 15. What number comes next?
items.why: When you count by 5s, you add 5 each time. 15 and 5 more is 20.

items.narration: Count by 10s. 10, 20. What number comes next? Is it 21, 25, or 30?
items.why: When you count by 10s, you add 10 each time. 20 and 10 more is 30.

items.narration: Count by 5s. Hop the frog from 0 to 35.
items.why: Hop by 5s. 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35. That is seven hops.

items.narration: Count by 2s. 12, 14, 16. What number comes next?
items.why: When you count by 2s, you add 2 each time. 16 and 2 more is 18.

items.narration: Count by 5s. 25, 30, 35. What number comes next? Is it 36, 40, or 45?
items.why: When you count by 5s, you add 5 each time. 35 and 5 more is 40.

items.narration: Count by 10s. 30, 40. What number comes next?
items.why: When you count by 10s, you add 10 each time. 40 and 10 more is 50.

items.narration: Count by 5s from 0. Do you land on 12, 15, 22, or 28?
items.why: Count by 5s. 5, 10, 15. You land on 15. The other numbers get skipped.

items.narration: Count by 2s. Hop the frog from 0 to 38.
items.why: Hop by 2s. 2, 4, 6, and on up to 38. Check that each hop adds 2.

items.narration: Count by 5s. 35, 40, then a missing number, then 50. What is the missing number?
items.why: Add 5 to 40 to get 45. Then 45 and 5 more is 50. It fits!

items.narration: Mia counts by 2s and stops at 50. When she counts by 2s, what number is just before 50? Is it 40, 45, 48, or 49?
items.why: Counting by 2s goes back 2 from 50. 50 take away 2 is 48.

items.narration: Each hand has 5 fingers. Here are 6 hands. Count by 5s. How many fingers in all?
items.why: Count by 5s once for each hand. 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30. That is 30 fingers.

items.narration: Start at 0. Hop 4 times. Each hop is 10. Where does the frog land?
items.why: Count by 10s for each hop. 10, 20, 30, 40. The frog lands on 40.

items.narration: Which number is greater, 7 or 12?
items.why: 12 has a ten and 7 does not. So 12 is greater than 7.

items.narration: Which number is less, 15 or 9?
items.why: 9 is only ones. 15 has a ten. So 9 is less than 15.

items.narration: Type the greater number, 6 or 11.
items.why: 11 comes after 6 when we count. Numbers later in counting are greater. So 11 is greater.

items.narration: Move the frog to the greater number, 5 or 13.
items.why: 13 is farther along the line than 5. The number farther along is greater.

items.narration: Which has more, 6 apples or 11 apples?
items.why: Count each pile. 11 is greater than 6. So 11 apples has more.

items.narration: Which number is greater, 34 or 28?
items.why: 34 has 3 tens. 28 has 2 tens. More tens means greater, so 34.

items.narration: Type the number that is less, 41 or 36.
items.why: 36 has 3 tens. 41 has 4 tens. Fewer tens means less, so 36.

items.narration: Move the frog to the least number, 44, 31, or 38.
items.why: Look at the tens. 31 has the fewest tens. So 31 is the least.

items.narration: Sam has 23 stickers. Mia has 32 stickers. Which number is less, 23 or 32?
items.why: 23 has 2 tens. 32 has 3 tens. So 23 is less.

items.narration: Put 25, 14, and 38 in order from least to greatest. Which number comes first?
items.why: Least to greatest starts with the smallest. 14 has just 1 ten. So 14 is first.

items.narration: Put 18, 42, and 27 in order from greatest to least. Type the number in the middle.
items.why: The order is 42, 27, 18. The number in the middle is 27.

items.narration: Which number is greater, 38 or 41?
items.why: Look at the tens first. 41 has 4 tens and 38 has 3 tens. So 41 is greater.

items.narration: Move the frog to the number between 38 and 40.
items.why: Count up from 38. The next number is 39. It is before 40.

items.narration: Three kids have 26, 19, and 33 cards. Type the fewest number of cards.
items.why: 19 has just 1 ten. 26 and 33 have more tens. So 19 is the least.

items.narration: Which list goes from greatest to least? Is it 9, 25, 40? Is it 40, 25, 9? Or is it 25, 40, 9?
items.why: Greatest to least starts with the biggest. 40 is first, then 25, then 9.

items.narration: Which number is 10 and 3? Is it 30, 13, or 8?
items.why: 10 and 3 more makes 13. Start at 10 and count up 3: 11, 12, 13.

items.narration: Mia has 10 stars in a box and 4 more. How many stars is that in all?
items.why: Start at 10 and count up 4 more: 11, 12, 13, 14. The answer is 14.

items.narration: Leo has 10 and 6 shells. Move the frog to the total number of shells.
items.why: 10 and 6 make 16. Start at 10 and hop 6 more.

items.narration: Which is the same as 12? Is it 10 and 2, or 10 and 5?
items.why: 12 is one ten and 2 ones. So 12 is 10 and 2.

items.narration: 15 is 10 and what? Type the missing part.
items.why: Take 10 away from 15. What is left is 5.

items.narration: 24 is 20 and what? Is it 14, 4, or 2?
items.why: Take 20 away from 24. That leaves 4.

items.narration: 20 and 7 make what number?
items.why: 20 is two tens. Add 7 ones to get 27.

items.narration: Lia has 20 and 9 shells. Move the frog to the total number of shells.
items.why: 20 and 9 make 29. Start at 20 and hop 9 more.

items.narration: Sam has 3 tens and 5 ones. What number is that? Is it 35, 53, or 8?
items.why: 3 tens is 30. Add 5 ones to make 35.

items.narration: Ben has 36 blocks. 36 is 30 and what? Type the missing part.
items.why: Take 30 away from 36. That leaves 6.

items.narration: Is 10 and 10 and 8 the same as 28? Is it No, or Yes?
items.why: 10 and 10 make 20. Then 20 and 8 make 28. So yes!

items.narration: 10 and 10 and 10 and 5 make what number?
items.why: Three 10s make 30. Then 30 and 5 make 35.

items.narration: Ava makes 9 groups of 5 beads. Move the frog to the total number of beads.
items.why: Count by 5s nine times. You land on 45.

items.narration: Which parts make 34? Is it 20 and 4, 30 and 14, or 30 and 4?
items.why: 3 tens is 30, and 4 ones is 4. So 30 and 4 make 34.

items.narration: Max has 4 tens and 7 ones. Move the frog to his number.
items.why: 4 tens is 40. Then add 7 ones to land on 47.

items.narration: Eight cookies are shared by 2 friends. How many cookies does each friend get? Is it 3, 5, 4, or 6?
items.why: Give one cookie to each friend again and again. Each friend gets 4 cookies.

items.narration: Two friends share these apples equally. How many apples does each friend get?
items.why: Share the apples one at a time. Each friend gets 3 apples.

items.narration: Four friends share 12 grapes equally. Hop the frog to how many grapes each friend gets.
items.why: Share 12 grapes with 4 friends. Each friend gets 3 grapes.

items.narration: Two friends share one pie. Which picture shows one half? Is it 1/2 of the circle, 1/4 of the circle, or 3/4 of the circle?
items.why: A half means 2 equal parts, and we take 1. That is the picture with 2 equal parts.

items.narration: Four friends share these grapes equally. How many grapes does each friend get?
items.why: Give each of the 4 friends one grape, then again. Each friend gets 2 grapes.

items.narration: Two friends share 5 cookies. Each gets 2 whole cookies. How many cookies are left to cut? Is it 0, 2, 3, or 1?
items.why: Each friend gets 2, so 4 cookies are given out. That leaves 1 cookie to cut in half.

items.narration: Two friends share 7 pears. Each friend gets some whole pears first. Hop the frog to how many whole pears each gets.
items.why: Give each friend 3 pears. That uses 6 pears. One pear is left to cut in half.

items.narration: Two friends share 3 cookies equally. How many cookies does each friend get? Is it 2, 1 1/2, or 1?
items.why: Each friend gets 1 whole cookie. The last cookie is cut in half. So each gets 1 and a half.

items.narration: A pan is cut into 8 equal parts. Four friends share the whole pan. How many parts does each friend get?
items.why: Share the 8 parts with 4 friends, one at a time. Each friend gets 2 parts.

items.narration: Four friends share this pizza. It has 4 equal slices. One slice is picked. What part of the pizza does each friend get? Is it 1/4, 1/2, or 3/4?
items.why: The pizza has 4 equal slices for 4 friends. Each friend gets 1 slice, which is 1/4.

items.narration: Four friends share 5 cookies equally. Each gets 1 whole cookie. The last cookie is cut in 4 equal parts. How much does each friend get? Is it 1 1/2, 1, 2, or 1 1/4?
items.why: Each friend gets 1 whole cookie. The last cookie is cut in 4 parts. So each gets one fourth more.

items.narration: Four friends share 14 sandwiches. Each friend gets 3 whole sandwiches. How many sandwiches are left over?
items.why: Four friends get 3 each, so 12 sandwiches are given out. That leaves 2 sandwiches.

items.narration: Two friends share 18 stickers equally. Hop the frog to how many stickers each friend gets.
items.why: Share the 18 stickers into 2 equal groups. Each friend gets 9 stickers.

items.narration: Four friends share one cookie. What does one friend get? Is it 1/2 of the circle, 3/4 of the circle, or 1/4 of the circle?
items.why: Four friends need 4 equal parts. One friend gets 1 of the 4 parts, which is one fourth.

items.narration: One pie is shared by 2 friends. A pie just like it is shared by 4 friends. Who gets bigger pieces, the 2 friends or the 4 friends?
items.why: With fewer friends, each piece is bigger. Two friends get halves, and four friends get fourths. A half is bigger.

items.narration: A pizza is cut into 2 equal slices. One slice is picked. What part is picked? Is it one half, one fourth, or one whole?
items.why: The pizza has 2 equal slices. One slice is one half.

items.narration: A pizza is cut into fourths. How many equal slices does it have?
items.why: Fourths means 4 equal parts. Count the slices to get 4.

items.narration: Two halves make one whole. Move the frog to how many halves make one whole.
items.why: One half and one half make a whole. So 2 halves make one whole.

items.narration: All 4 fourths of a pizza are picked. What do you have? Is it one fourth, one half, or one whole?
items.why: Four fourths fill the whole pizza. So you have one whole.

items.narration: Two halves make one whole. How many halves are picked here?
items.why: The pizza has 2 halves and both are picked. So the answer is 2.

items.narration: A pizza has 4 equal slices. 2 slices are picked. Which is the same amount as the 2 picked slices? Is it one half, one fourth, or one whole?
items.why: Two fourths is the same as one half of the pizza.

items.narration: Four fourths make one whole. Move the frog to how many fourths make one whole.
items.why: A whole cut in fourths has 4 equal parts. So 4 fourths make one whole.

items.narration: Sam eats one half of a pan of brownies. The pan has 4 equal pieces. How many pieces does Sam eat?
items.why: One half is the same as two fourths. So Sam eats 2 pieces.

items.narration: Which picture shows one half of a pan of brownies? Is it 1/4 of the pan, 3/4 of the pan, or 2/4 of the pan?
items.why: Two out of four equal pieces is one half. It is the same amount.

items.narration: Is one half the same as two fourths of one pizza? Yes or no?
items.why: Cut one half in two equal parts and you get two fourths. So yes, they are the same.

items.narration: Ana eats 2 fourths of a pie. Her friend eats one half of the same pie. How many fourths does her friend eat?
items.why: One half is the same as 2 fourths. So her friend eats 2 fourths.

items.narration: Mia keeps one half of a pizza. She cuts it into fourths. Move the frog to how many fourths she keeps.
items.prompt: One half is how many fourths?
items.why: One half is the same as 2 fourths. So Mia keeps 2 fourths.

items.narration: Mia eats 2 fourths of a pizza. Jay eats one half of the same pizza. Who eats more? Is it Mia, Jay, or the same amount?
items.why: Two fourths is the same as one half. So they eat the same amount.

items.narration: A pan is cut into 4 equal pieces. You want one half of the pan. How many pieces do you take? Is it 1, 3, 4, or 2?
items.why: One half is the same as two fourths. So take 2 pieces.

items.narration: A pizza has 2 halves. Mia cuts each half into 2 equal slices. How many slices are there in all?
items.why: Each half makes 2 slices. 2 + 2 = 4, so there are 4 fourths.

items.narration: Which is the bigger piece: 1/2 of the circle or 1/4 of the circle?
items.why: Fewer kids share, so each piece is bigger. A half is bigger than a fourth.

items.narration: Which is the smaller piece: 1/2 of the circle or 1/8 of the circle?
items.why: More kids share, so each piece is smaller. An eighth is smaller than a half.

items.narration: A pizza is cut into 4 equal slices. Each kid gets one slice. How many kids share this pizza?
items.why: The pizza has 4 equal slices. Each kid gets one slice, so 4 kids share it.

items.narration: A pizza is cut into 6 equal slices. Move the frog to the number of slices.
items.why: The pizza has 6 slices, so the frog goes to 6.

items.narration: Two kids share a pizza, or four kids share the same pizza. Who gets the bigger piece: 2 kids or 4 kids?
items.why: Fewer kids means bigger pieces. When 2 kids share, each piece is a half.

items.narration: Which piece is the biggest: 1/3 of the circle, 1/2 of the circle, or 1/6 of the circle?
items.why: The fewest parts make the biggest piece. A half has only 2 parts, so it is biggest.

items.narration: Who gets the smallest piece of the same bar: 3 kids, 5 kids, or 4 kids?
items.why: The most kids make the smallest piece. 5 kids is the most, so a fifth is smallest.

items.narration: This bar is cut into 10 equal parts. Each kid gets one part. How many kids share the bar?
items.why: The bar has 10 equal parts. Each kid gets one part, so 10 kids share it.

items.narration: Mia cuts her bar into 3 parts. Sam wants smaller parts. He cuts 2 more parts than Mia. Move the frog to Sam's parts.
items.why: Mia has 3 parts. Sam has 2 more, so 3 + 2 = 5 parts.

items.narration: Is 1/5 of a pizza bigger than 1/8 of the same pizza? Yes or No?
items.why: Sharing with 5 gives bigger pieces than sharing with 8. So 1/5 is bigger.

items.narration: Which is the smallest piece: 1/10 of the circle, 1/4 of the circle, or 1/6 of the circle?
items.why: The most parts make the smallest piece. A circle cut in 10 parts has the tiniest pieces.

items.narration: 8 kids share this bar. Each gets one part. Then 2 kids leave. How many kids share the bar now?
items.why: There were 8 kids. Two left, so 8 - 2 = 6 kids share the bar.

items.narration: Six kids share a pan. Add kids so pieces get smaller. Move the frog to the fewest kids that works.
items.why: More kids make smaller pieces. One more than 6 is 7, so the frog goes to 7.

items.narration: Mia gets 1/4 of a bar. Leo wants a smaller piece. Should his bar be shared by 3 kids or 6 kids?
items.prompt: Who shares for a smaller piece?
items.why: Sharing with 6 gives smaller pieces than sharing with 4. A sixth is smaller than a fourth.

items.narration: A pizza is shared by 3 kids. Then twice as many kids share it. Move the frog to the new number of kids.
items.why: Twice 3 is 6. So 6 kids share it, and each piece is smaller.

items.narration: What is 3 + 2? Is it 4, 5, or 6?
items.why: Start at 3 and count up 2 more. 4, 5. The answer is 5.

items.narration: Sam has 4 fish. 1 more fish swims in. How many fish are there now?
items.why: One more than 4 is 5. So 4 + 1 = 5.

items.narration: Move the frog to the answer of 5 + 2.
items.why: Start at 5. Hop 2 times to the right. You land on 7.

items.narration: What is 5 - 2? That is 5 take away 2. Is it 2, 4, or 3?
items.why: Start with 5. Take away 2. 4, 3. You have 3 left.

items.narration: What is 5 + 5?
items.why: Two groups of 5 make 10. So 5 + 5 = 10.

items.narration: What is 7 + 2? Is it 9, 8, or 10?
items.why: Start at 7. Count up 2. 8, 9. The answer is 9.

items.narration: What is 9 - 4? That is 9 take away 4.
items.why: 4 and 5 make 9. So 9 take away 4 is 5.

items.narration: Move the frog to the answer of 8 - 5. That is 8 take away 5.
items.why: Start at 8. Hop back 5 times. You land on 3.

items.narration: 4 and what number make 10? Is it 5, 7, 4, or 6?
items.why: 4 and 6 make 10. Count up from 4 to 10. That is 6 steps.

items.narration: The ten frame has 7 dots. How many more dots make 10?
items.why: The ten frame has 3 empty spots. 7 and 3 make 10.

items.narration: Sam knows 3 + 6 = 9. Is it true or false that 9 take away 3 is 6?
items.why: 3 and 6 make 9. So 9 take away 3 is 6. It is true.

items.narration: What number and 3 make 10?
items.why: Start at 10 and take away 3. That leaves 7. So 7 and 3 make 10.

items.narration: The frog starts at 10. Take away 6. Move the frog to the answer.
items.why: 6 and 4 make 10. So 10 take away 6 is 4.

items.narration: Which is greatest: 6 + 3, 4 + 4, or 5 + 5?
items.why: 6 + 3 is 9. 4 + 4 is 8. 5 + 5 is 10. So 5 + 5 is greatest.

items.narration: Ana has 8 stickers. She gives 3 away. Then she gets 2 more. How many stickers does she have now?
items.why: 8 take away 3 is 5. Then 5 and 2 more make 7.

items.narration: What is 6 + 0?
items.why: Adding 0 adds nothing. So 6 + 0 stays 6.

items.narration: We know 2 + 5 = 7. What is 5 + 2? Is it 8, 7, or 6?
items.why: Adding in any order gives the same total. 5 + 2 is 7, just like 2 + 5.

items.narration: What is 8 - 0? Hop the frog to the answer.
items.why: Taking away 0 changes nothing. 8 - 0 is still 8.

items.narration: Mia has 4 apples. She adds 0 more. How many apples does she have now? Is it 0, 5, or 4?
items.why: Adding 0 means no more apples. She still has 4.

items.narration: 3 + 4 = 4 + what number?
items.why: Both sides use the same two numbers. Swap 3 and 4 to see the missing number is 3.

items.narration: We know 9 - 4 = 5. Which one checks it? Is it 5 + 4 = 9, 5 + 5 = 10, or 9 + 4 = 13?
items.why: To check, add the answer 5 and the 4 you took away. 5 + 4 = 9, which is where we began.

items.narration: We know 8 + 7 = 15. So what is 7 + 8?
items.why: Order does not matter when adding. 7 + 8 is the same as 8 + 7, so it is 15.

items.narration: We know 13 - 6 = 7. To check, hop the frog to 7 + 6.
items.why: Add the answer 7 and the 6 you took away. 7 + 6 is 13, the number we began with.

items.narration: We know 12 - 5 = 7. To check, what is 7 + 5?
items.why: Add the answer back to the part you took away. 7 + 5 is 12, so the take-away was right.

items.narration: Which one is the same as 6 + 9? Is it 9 + 6, 6 + 6, or 9 - 6?
items.why: Swapping the numbers in an add gives the same total. 9 + 6 is the same as 6 + 9.

items.narration: A number plus 8 is the same as 8 + 11. What is the missing number?
items.why: Adding in any order gives the same total. So the missing number is 11.

items.narration: Sam thinks 15 - 6 = 8. Add 8 + 6 to check. Is Sam right, yes or no?
items.why: 8 + 6 is 14, not 15. So 15 - 6 is not 8. It is 9.

items.narration: Start at 17. Add 0. Then take away 0. Where does the frog land?
items.why: Adding 0 and taking away 0 change nothing. The frog stays on 17.

items.narration: Ana gave away 8 stickers. Now she has 9 left. How many did she start with?
items.why: Use adding to undo the take-away. Add the 9 left and the 8 given away to get 17.

items.narration: Which total is greatest? Is it 8 + 0, 9 + 0, or 2 + 6?
items.why: 8 + 0 is 8 and 9 + 0 is 9. Also 2 + 6 is 8. So 9 + 0 is greatest.

items.narration: Count on from 7. What is 7 + 2?
items.why: Start at 7 and count on 2. That is 8, then 9. The answer is 9.

items.narration: What is 9 + 1? Is it 8, 10, or 11?
items.why: 9 and 1 more makes 10. Nine is just one away from 10.

items.narration: Move the frog to the answer of 6 + 4.
items.why: 6 and 4 make 10. Hop from 6 four times to reach 10.

items.narration: Mia has 10 grapes and eats 4. How many are left? Is it 6, 4, or 5?
items.why: Count back 4 from 10. That is 9, 8, 7, 6. So 6 are left.

items.narration: Here are 8 apples. Mia gets 2 more. How many apples does she have now?
items.why: 8 and 2 make 10. Count on from 8: 9, 10.

items.narration: Make 10 first. What is 8 + 5? Is it 12, 13, or 14?
items.why: Take 2 from the 5 to make 10 with 8. Then add the 3 left. 10 and 3 is 13.

items.narration: Double 6 is 12. Now use it. What is 6 + 7?
items.why: Double 6 is 12. Seven is one more than 6, so add 1 to get 13.

items.narration: Move the frog to the answer of 15 - 6.
items.why: Think: 6 and what make 15? Six and 9 make 15. So 15 - 6 is 9.

items.narration: Mia has 14 plums and eats 5. How many are left? Is it 8, 9, or 10?
items.why: Take 4 to get to 10. Then take 1 more. 10 take away 1 is 9.

items.narration: Double 8 is 16. Use it. What is 16 - 8?
items.why: Two 8s make 16. So if you take away one 8, one 8 is left.

items.narration: Use near doubles or make 10. What is 7 + 8?
items.why: Double 7 is 14. Eight is one more than 7. So 14 and 1 is 15.

items.narration: Move the frog to the answer of 9 + 8.
items.why: Take 1 from the 8 to make 10 with 9. Then add the 7 left. 10 and 7 is 17.

items.narration: Is 6 + 7 the same as 6 + 6 + 1? Yes or no?
items.why: Seven is 6 and 1 more. So 6 + 7 is double 6, plus 1. The answer is yes.

items.narration: Think: 9 and what make 17? Use it to find 17 - 9.
items.why: Nine and 8 make 17. So 17 take away 9 is 8.

items.narration: Mia has 13 grapes and eats 8. How many are left? Is it 6, 4, or 5?
items.why: Think: 8 and 5 make 13. So 13 take away 8 is 5.

items.narration: Ben has 8 toy cars. He gets 3 more. How many cars does he have now? Is it 10, 11, 12, or 13?
items.why: Start at 8 and count on 3 more. 9, 10, 11. Ben has 11 cars.

items.narration: Ana has 25 stickers. She gets 6 more. How many stickers does she have now? Is it 29, 30, 31, or 32?
items.why: Add 5 to make 30. Then add 1 more. 25 + 6 is 31.

items.narration: Leo has 34 shells. Zoe has 28 shells. How many more shells does Leo have? Is it 5, 6, 7, or 8?
items.why: Count up from 28 to 30 is 2. Then 30 to 34 is 4. That is 6 more.

items.narration: Some birds sat on a fence. Then 7 more came. Now there are 15 birds. How many were there at first? Is it 6, 8, 9, or 22?
items.why: Take 7 from 15 to go back to the start. 15 - 7 = 8 birds.

items.narration: Tom has 9 grapes. He eats 4 of them. Which number sentence shows how many are left? Is it 9 + 4 = 13, or 9 - 4 = 5?
items.why: Eating takes grapes away. So we subtract. 9 - 4 = 5 grapes are left.

items.narration: Here are 6 fish. 4 more fish swim in. How many fish are there now?
items.why: Start at 6 and count on 4. 7, 8, 9, 10. There are 10 fish.

items.narration: Kai has 10 coins. He spends 3 coins. How many coins does he have left?
items.why: Take away 3 from 10. Count back: 9, 8, 7. Kai has 7 coins.

items.narration: There are 23 kids on a bus. 5 more kids get on. How many kids are on the bus now?
Mia has 36 beads. She uses 12 beads for a bracelet. How many beads are left?
items.why: Take away 10 first to get 26. Then take away 2 more. 24 beads are left.

items.narration: Dan had some cards. He got 14 more. Now he has 40 cards. How many cards did he have at first?
items.why: Go back from 40 by taking away 14. 40 - 14 = 26 cards.

items.narration: The frog starts at 5. It hops 4 more. Drag the frog to where it lands.
items.why: Start at 5. Hop 4 times to the right: 6, 7, 8, 9.

items.narration: The frog starts at 20. It hops back 6. Drag the frog to where it lands.
items.why: Hop back to the left 6 times from 20. You land on 14.

items.narration: Pip has 30 stones. He finds 15 more. Drag the frog to how many stones he has now.
items.why: Each hop is 5. From 30, two hops make 40, and one more hop makes 45.

items.narration: There are 50 birds in a tree. 18 birds fly away. Drag the frog to how many birds are left.
items.why: Take away 20 to get 30. That was 2 too many, so add 2 back. 32 birds are left.

items.narration: Zed has 27 marbles. He wants 35 marbles. How many more does he need? Drag the frog to the answer.
items.why: Count up from 27 to 30 is 3. Then 30 to 35 is 5. That is 8 more.

items.narration: There are 2 groups of 2 stars. How many stars in all? Is it 3, 4, or 5?
items.why: Count by 2s. 2, 4. So there are 4 stars in all.

items.narration: There are 3 bowls with 2 fish in each bowl. How many fish in all?
items.why: Count by 2s. 2, 4, 6. There are 6 fish.

items.narration: Sam has 3 cups. Each cup has 2 straws. Move the frog to how many straws in all.
items.why: Count by 2s. 2, 4, 6. Sam has 6 straws.

items.narration: A pie is cut into halves. How many halves make the whole pie? Is it 2, 1, or 3?
items.why: The pie has 2 equal parts. Each part is one half. So 2 halves make the whole pie.

items.narration: Here are 6 cookies. Each plate gets 2 cookies. How many plates? Is it 3, 2, or 4?
items.why: Make groups of 2. 2, 4, 6. That is 3 groups, so 3 plates.

items.narration: There are 4 leaves. Each leaf has 2 bugs on it. How many bugs in all?
items.why: Count by 2s. 2, 4, 6, 8. There are 8 bugs.

items.narration: Lena has 5 bags. Each bag has 2 apples. Move the frog to how many apples in all.
items.why: Count by 2s. 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. Lena has 10 apples.

items.narration: Here are 8 grapes. Each cup gets 2 grapes. How many cups? Is it 2, 6, or 4?
items.why: Make groups of 2. 2, 4, 6, 8. That is 4 groups, so 4 cups.

items.narration: Here are 3 sandwiches. Each one is cut into halves. All the halves are colored in. How many halves in all?
items.why: Each sandwich has 2 halves. Count by 2s. 2, 4, 6. There are 6 halves.

items.narration: Ben has 3 groups of 3 stickers. How many stickers in all? Is it 9, 6, or 8?
items.why: Count by 3s. 3, 6, 9. Ben has 9 stickers.

items.narration: Tia has 10 crackers. She puts 2 crackers on each plate. Move the frog to how many plates.
items.why: Count by 2s. 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. That took 5 counts, so 5 plates.

items.narration: Here are 9 apples. Each bag holds 3 apples. How many bags?
items.why: Make groups of 3. 3, 6, 9. That is 3 groups, so 3 bags.

items.narration: Which story makes 10 in all? Is it 3 groups of 3, 5 groups of 2, or 4 groups of 2?
items.why: Count by 2s five times. 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. So 5 groups of 2 makes 10.

items.narration: Kim has 10 crackers. She puts 5 crackers on each plate. How many plates does she fill?
items.why: Count by 5s. 5, 10. That is 2 groups, so 2 plates.

items.narration: Zed ate the picked halves of toast. How many halves did Zed eat? Is it 10, 6, or 5?
items.why: Each colored part is one half. Count them. 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Zed ate 5 halves.

items.narration: Pia has 1 hundred, 4 tens, and 2 ones. What number is that?
items.why: 1 hundred is 100. 4 tens is 40. 2 ones is 2. Put them together to get 142.

items.narration: How many tens make one hundred? Is it 5, 10, 20, or 100?
items.why: Ten tens make one hundred. Count by tens ten times to reach 100.

items.narration: Move the frog to 150.
items.why: 150 is halfway between 100 and 200. Count by tens from 100: 110, 120, 130, 140, 150.

items.narration: Which number is one hundred twenty-six? Is it 162, 126, or 106?
items.why: One hundred twenty-six is 1 hundred, 2 tens, and 6 ones. That is 126.

items.narration: What is 100 + 7?
items.why: There are no tens. So 1 hundred and 7 ones is 107.

items.narration: Sam has 150 beads. How many tens is that?
items.why: 10 tens make 100. 5 more tens make 50. So 150 is 15 tens.

items.narration: 124 is 100 and how many more? Is it 24, 42, 4, or 12?
items.why: Take away the 100 from 124. What is left is 24.

items.narration: Move the frog to 165.
items.why: 165 is 1 hundred, 6 tens, and 5 ones. Go to 160, then 5 more.

items.narration: 12 tens and 5 ones is the same as 152. Is that true or false?
items.why: 12 tens is 120. Add 5 ones to get 125, not 152. So it is false.

items.narration: A box holds 10 pencils. Sam has 14 boxes. How many pencils is that?
items.why: 14 tens is 10 tens and 4 tens. That is 100 and 40, so 140.

items.narration: Mia has 9 tens and 15 ones. What number is that?
items.why: 9 tens is 90. 15 ones is 10 and 5. So 90 and 10 make 100, and 5 more is 105.

items.narration: Which number is the same as 17 tens and 6 ones? Is it 167, 176, or 76?
items.why: 17 tens is 170. Add 6 ones to get 176.

items.narration: Move the frog to the number with 17 tens and 5 ones.
items.why: 17 tens is 170. Add 5 ones to land on 175.

items.narration: 164 is 1 hundred, 5 tens, and how many ones?
items.why: 100 and 50 make 150. From 150 to 164 is 14 more. So there are 14 ones.

items.narration: Which is greatest, 1 hundred 9 tens, 18 tens 5 ones, or 17 tens 9 ones?
items.why: 1 hundred 9 tens is 190. 18 tens 5 ones is 185. 17 tens 9 ones is 179. So 190 is greatest.

items.narration: Which number is greater, 87 or 120?
items.why: 120 has 1 hundred. 87 has no hundreds. So 120 is greater than 87.

items.narration: Which number is less, 150 or 105?
items.why: Both have 1 hundred. 105 has 0 tens and 150 has 5 tens. So 105 is less.

items.narration: Is 190 closer to 100 or closer to 200?
items.why: 190 is only 10 away from 200. It is 90 away from 100. So it is closer to 200.

items.narration: Which number is greater, 94 or 149? Type the greater number.
items.why: 149 has 1 hundred. 94 has none. So 149 is the greater number.

items.narration: Move the frog to 100.
items.why: 100 is halfway between 0 and 200. Count the jumps of 50 to find it.

items.narration: Which number is the greatest, 138, 183, or 118?
items.why: All have 1 hundred. Now check the tens. 8 tens is more than 3 tens or 1 ten. So 183 is greatest.

items.narration: Mia puts 150, 105, and 115 in order from least to greatest. Which number goes first?
items.why: Least to greatest starts with the smallest. 105 has the fewest tens. So 105 goes first.

items.narration: Here are 163, 136, and 183. Type the least number.
items.why: All have 1 hundred. 136 has 3 tens. The others have more tens. So 136 is least.

items.narration: Put 120, 87, and 150 in order from least to greatest. Type the middle number.
items.why: The order is 87, then 120, then 150. The middle number is 120.

items.narration: Here are 140, 90, and 120. Move the frog to the least number.
items.why: 90 has no hundreds. 140 and 120 each have 1 hundred. So 90 is the least.

items.narration: True or false? 99 is greater than 101.
items.why: 101 has 1 hundred. 99 has none. So 101 is greater, and the sentence is false.

items.narration: Here are 175, 157, 171, and 177. Type the greatest number.
items.why: All have 1 hundred and 7 or 5 tens. Compare the ones in 175, 171, and 177. 177 is greatest.

items.narration: Type the number that is greater than 168 and less than 170.
items.why: Count up from 168. The next number is 169. Then comes 170. So 169 is between them.

items.narration: Here are 165, 156, and 175. Move the frog to the greatest number.
items.why: All have 1 hundred. 175 has 7 tens. The others have 6 tens or 5 tens. So 175 is greatest.

items.narration: Here are 60, 180, and 120. Move the frog to the middle number when they go from least to greatest.
items.why: The order is 60, then 120, then 180. The middle number is 120.

items.narration: 6 cookies are shared by 2 friends. How many cookies does each friend get? Is it 2, 4, 3, or 6?
items.why: Give each friend one cookie at a time. After 3 rounds, all 6 cookies are gone. Each friend gets 3.

items.narration: 8 apples are shared by 4 friends. How many apples does each friend get?
items.why: Hand out 1 apple to each of the 4 friends. Do it again. That uses all 8. Each gets 2.

items.narration: 10 stickers are shared by 2 friends. Drag the frog to how many stickers each friend gets.
items.why: Split the 10 stickers into 2 equal groups. Each group has 5 stickers.

items.narration: 4 bars are shared by 3 friends. Each gets 1 bar. One bar is left. Into how many equal parts do we cut it? Is it 2, 3, 4, or 6?
items.prompt: Cut the left bar into how many parts?
items.why: There are 3 friends. So the left bar is cut into 3 equal parts. Each friend gets one part.

items.narration: 9 pears are shared by 3 friends. How many pears does each friend get?
items.why: Make 3 equal groups from 9 pears. Each group has 3 pears.

items.narration: 4 sandwiches are shared by 3 friends. How much does each friend get? Is it 1 1/3, 1 1/2, 2, or 1 2/3?
items.why: Each friend gets 1 whole sandwich. One is left. Cut it in 3 parts. Each friend gets 1 and one third.

items.narration: 7 crackers are shared by 3 friends. How many whole crackers does each friend get? Drag the frog to the number.
items.why: Each friend gets 2 crackers. That uses 6. One cracker is left to cut up.

items.narration: One pie is cut into 4 equal parts. 4 friends share it. What part does each friend get? Is it 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, or 2/3?
items.why: The pie has 4 equal parts for 4 friends. Each friend gets 1 part. That is 1/4.

items.narration: 5 cookies are shared by 2 friends. How much does each friend get? Is it 2, 2 1/2, 3, or 2 1/4?
items.why: Each friend gets 2 whole cookies. One is left. Cut it in halves. Each friend gets 2 and one half.

items.narration: 10 bars are shared by 3 friends. Each friend gets 3 whole bars. How many bars are left over?
items.why: 3 friends each get 3 bars. That is 9 bars. 10 take away 9 leaves 1 bar.

items.narration: 2 bars are shared by 3 friends. Each bar is cut into 3 equal parts. How much does each friend get? Is it 1/3, 1/2, 2/3, or 2?
items.why: Cut each bar into thirds. Each friend takes one third from each bar. That is 2 thirds.

items.narration: Some bars were shared by 3 friends. Each friend got 3 and one third bars. How many bars were there?
items.why: 3 friends each got 3 whole bars. That is 9 bars. The 3 thirds make 1 more bar. 9 + 1 = 10.

items.narration: 10 bars can be shared by 3 friends or by 6 friends. Who gets more each? 3 friends or 6 friends?
items.why: With fewer friends, each share is bigger. 10 bars shared by 3 friends gives more than by 6 friends.

items.narration: 10 granola bars are shared by 3 friends. How much does each friend get? Is it 3, 3 2/3, 5, or 3 1/3?
items.why: Each friend gets 3 whole bars. That uses 9. One bar is left. Cut it in thirds. Each gets 3 and one third.

items.narration: 10 bars are shared by 6 friends. Each friend gets 1 whole bar first. How many bars are left? Drag the frog to the number.
items.why: 6 friends each get 1 bar. That uses 6 bars. 10 take away 6 leaves 4 bars to cut up.

items.narration: A pizza is cut into 3 equal slices. One slice is picked. What fraction is picked? Is it 1/6, 1/2, or 1/3?
items.why: The pizza has 3 equal slices and 1 is picked. So one third is picked.

items.narration: Mia cuts a pizza into sixths. That means equal slices. How many slices does the pizza have?
items.why: Sixths means 6 equal slices. You can count them in the picture too. There are 6.

items.narration: Three thirds make one whole pizza. A pizza is cut into thirds. How many slices make the whole pizza?
items.why: Thirds means 3 equal slices. All 3 slices make the whole pizza.

items.narration: Which picture shows one third of a pizza? Is it 1 of 6 parts picked, 1 of 3 parts picked, or 1 of 2 parts picked?
items.why: One third means 1 of 3 equal slices. The pizza cut into 3 slices with 1 picked shows it.

items.narration: A pizza is cut into 6 equal slices. Two of the 6 slices are picked. How many sixths are picked?
items.why: Two slices are picked. Each slice is one sixth, so two sixths are picked.

items.narration: Leo eats one third of a pizza. Which is the same amount of that pizza? Is it 1/6, 3/6, or 2/6?
items.why: Cut each third into 2 sixths. One third is 2 sixths.

items.narration: One third of a pizza equals how many sixths of that pizza?
items.why: Each third can be cut into 2 sixths. So one third equals 2 sixths.

items.narration: Two thirds of a pizza equals how many sixths of it?
items.why: Each third is 2 sixths. Two thirds is 2 and 2 more, which is 4 sixths.

items.narration: Is one sixth of a pizza equal to one third of it? Yes or no?
items.why: One sixth is a small slice. One third is bigger. Two sixths would equal one third.

items.narration: Two sixths of this pizza are picked. Cut the same pizza into 3 equal slices instead. How many thirds are picked?
items.why: Two sixths is the same amount as one third. So 1 slice is picked.

items.narration: This strip has 4 sixths picked. Which fraction is the same amount? Is it 1/3, 1/2, or 2/3?
items.why: Every 2 sixths make 1 third. So 4 sixths make 2 thirds.

items.narration: Ben ate 4 sixths of a pan of brownies. That is the same as how many thirds of the pan?
items.why: Two sixths make one third. Four sixths make two groups, so 2 thirds.

items.narration: Three friends each eat one third of a pizza. The pizza is cut in sixths. How many sixths do they eat all together?
items.why: Each friend eats 2 sixths. Three friends eat 3 times 2, which is 6 sixths.

items.narration: Mia ate 2/6 of a pizza. Leo ate 1/3 of the same pizza. Who ate more? Mia ate more, Leo ate more, or same amount?
items.why: Two sixths is the same as one third. So they ate the same amount.

items.narration: A pizza is cut into 6 equal slices. Zoe eats one third of the pizza. How many sixths are left?
items.why: One third is 2 sixths. Take 2 slices from 6 and 4 are left.

items.narration: You know 5 + 3 = 8. What is 3 + 5? Is it 5, 3, 8, or 9?
items.why: Adding in any order gives the same answer. 5 + 3 and 3 + 5 are both 8.

items.narration: What is 6 + 0?
items.why: Adding zero changes nothing. 6 plus 0 is still 6.

items.narration: Move the frog to the answer of 4 + 3.
items.why: Start at 4 and hop 3 more. 4, 5, 6, 7. The answer is 7.

items.narration: Frog hops 2, then 2, then 2. How far did it go in all? Is it 6, 5, 4, or 8?
items.why: Add the equal jumps. 2 and 2 is 4. Then 4 and 2 is 6.

items.narration: What is 8 - 0?
items.why: Taking away zero changes nothing. 8 take away 0 is still 8.

items.narration: Is 8 + 6 the same as 6 + 8? Yes or no?
items.why: Adding in any order gives the same answer. Both 8 + 6 and 6 + 8 make 14.

items.narration: You know 12 - 5 = 7. Add to check. What is 7 + 5?
items.why: Adding back what you took away gets you to the start. 7 + 5 is 12.

items.narration: Move the frog to the answer of 15 - 0.
items.why: Taking away zero changes nothing. So 15 - 0 is 15.

items.narration: We know 14 - 6 = 8. Which sentence checks it? Is it 8 + 6 = 14, 8 + 8 = 16, 14 + 6 = 20, or 6 + 6 = 12?
items.why: To check, add the answer to the part you took away. 8 + 6 makes 14.

items.narration: Sam hops 5, then 5, then 5. How far did he go in all?
items.why: Add the equal jumps. 5 and 5 is 10. Then 10 and 5 is 15.

items.narration: Ben gave away 8 stickers. He has 9 left. How many did he have at the start?
items.why: Add the stickers back to check. 9 left plus 8 given away is 17.

items.narration: Mia adds 6 + 9 + 4. What is the total? Is it 18, 19, 20, or 21?
items.why: Add in any order. Make a ten first: 6 + 4 is 10. Then 10 + 9 is 19.

items.narration: Frog starts at 0 and jumps by 5, four times. Move the frog to where it lands.
items.why: Count the jumps: 5, 10, 15, 20. Four jumps of 5 land on 20.

items.narration: Which is the same as 4 + 4 + 4? Is it 3 jumps of 4, 3 jumps of 3, 4 jumps of 4, or 2 jumps of 4?
items.why: 4 + 4 + 4 has three equal groups of 4. That is 3 jumps of 4, which makes 12.

items.narration: Lia found that 25 - 9 = 16. Add to check it. What is 16 + 9?
items.why: Add the answer to the part taken away. 16 + 9 is 25, so Lia is right.

items.narration: What is 5 + 5? Is it 8, 10, or 12?
items.why: 5 and 5 is a double. Count 5, then 5 more. You get 10.

items.narration: Jo has 6 stars. Jo gets 3 more stars. How many stars now?
items.why: Start at 6. Count up 3 more: 7, 8, 9. The answer is 9.

items.narration: Move the frog to the answer of 4 + 5.
items.why: Start at 4 and hop 5 times. You land on 9.

items.narration: What is 10 - 4? Is it 5, 6, or 7?
There are 9 birds. 5 birds fly away. How many birds are left?
What is 8 + 8? Is it 14, 18, or 16?
items.why: 8 and 8 is a double. Double 8 is 16.

items.narration: What is 9 + 5? Make 10 first.
items.why: Take 1 from 5 to make 9 into 10. Then 10 + 4 = 14.

items.narration: Move the frog to the answer of 12 - 5.
What is 14 - 6? Is it 7, 8, 9, or 10?
items.why: Go back to 10 first. 14 - 4 = 10. Then take away 2 more to get 8.

items.narration: What is 7 + 8? Use a double to help.
items.why: 7 + 7 = 14. Then add 1 more. The answer is 15.

items.narration: 8 + 9 = 17. Which take-away fact goes with it? Is it 17 - 9 = 8, 17 - 8 = 8, or 17 - 7 = 9?
items.why: Take one part away from 17 to get the other part. 17 - 9 = 8.

items.narration: 8 plus what number makes 15? Find the missing number.
items.why: Count up from 8 to 10. That is 2. Then 5 more to reach 15. 2 + 5 = 7.

items.narration: Move the frog to the answer of 16 - 7.
Which sum is greatest? Is it 7 + 7, 6 + 9, or 8 + 6?
Sam has 20 stickers. Sam gives away 12 stickers. How many stickers are left?
items.why: Think 12 + 8 = 20. So Sam has 8 stickers left.

items.narration: Here are 4 ducks. Each duck has 2 legs. How many legs in all?
items.why: Add 2 four times. 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 8. So there are 8 legs.

items.narration: Mia has 3 groups of 4 cookies. Which adds up to 3 groups of 4? Is it 3 + 4, 4 + 4, or 4 + 4 + 4?
items.why: 3 groups of 4 means you add 4 three times. That is 4 + 4 + 4.

items.narration: Frog hops 2 at a time. It makes 3 hops from 0. Move the frog to where it lands.
items.why: Hop 2, then 4, then 6. 2 + 2 + 2 = 6.

items.narration: Here are 3 hands. Each hand has 5 fingers. How many fingers in all?
items.why: Add 5 three times. 5 + 5 + 5 = 15. So there are 15 fingers.

items.narration: A pizza is cut into 4 equal slices. Each slice is one fourth. How many fourths make 1 whole pizza? Is it 4, 8, or 2?
items.why: The pizza has 4 equal slices. All 4 fourths together make 1 whole pizza.

items.narration: Leo has 6 bags. Each bag has 3 apples. How many apples in all?
items.why: Add 3 six times. 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 18. Leo has 18 apples.

items.narration: Frog hops 5 at a time. It makes 7 hops from 0. Move the frog to where it lands.
items.why: Count by 5s seven times. 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35. The frog lands on 35.

items.narration: A tricycle has 3 wheels. There are 4 tricycles. How many wheels in all? Is it 7, 12, or 9?
items.why: Add 3 four times. 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12. There are 12 wheels.

items.narration: Here are 2 pizzas. Each pizza is cut into 4 equal slices. Eight slices are picked. That is 8 groups of one fourth. How many whole pizzas is that?
items.why: Every 4 fourths make 1 whole pizza. 8 fourths is 2 groups of 4. So it is 2 wholes.

items.narration: Ben has 4 feet. Each foot has 5 toes. How many toes in all? Is it 9, 15, 20, or 25?
items.why: Add 5 four times. 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 = 20. Ben has 20 toes.

items.narration: Frog hops one half at a time. It makes 8 hops from 0. Move the frog to where it lands.
items.why: Two hops of one half make 1. Eight hops make 4 groups of 2 hops, so the frog lands on 4.

items.narration: A half carton holds 6 eggs. Sam has 7 half cartons. How many eggs in all?
items.why: Add 6 seven times. 6 + 6 + 6 + 6 + 6 + 6 + 6 = 42. Sam has 42 eggs.

items.narration: Which makes the most? Is it 5 groups of 2, 3 groups of 5, or 4 groups of 3?
items.why: 5 groups of 2 is 10. 3 groups of 5 is 15. 4 groups of 3 is 12. So 15 is the most.

items.narration: Here are 3 pizzas. Each pizza is cut into 4 equal slices. Every slice is one fourth. How many fourths in all?
items.why: Each pizza has 4 fourths. Add 4 three times. 4 + 4 + 4 = 12 fourths.

items.narration: Frog hops 4 at a time. It makes 8 hops from 0. Move the frog to where it lands.
items.why: Count by 4s eight times. 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 28, 32. The frog lands on 32.

items.narration: Mia shares 6 apples equally between 2 friends. How many apples does each friend get? Is it 2, 3, or 4?
items.why: Give one apple to each friend again and again. Each friend gets 3 apples.

items.narration: Ben has 10 cookies. He shares them equally on 2 plates. How many cookies are on each plate?
items.why: Share the cookies one at a time to each plate. Each plate gets 5 cookies.

items.narration: Eight stickers are shared equally by 4 friends. Move the frog to how many stickers each friend gets.
items.why: Share 8 stickers with 4 friends, one at a time. Each friend gets 2 stickers.

items.narration: Sam has 6 fish. He puts 2 fish in each bowl. How many bowls does he fill?
items.why: Count by 2s. 2, 4, 6. That is 3 bowls.

items.narration: Zoe has 4 balloons. She shares them equally between 2 kids. How many balloons does each kid get? Is it 1, 3, or 2?
items.why: Give one balloon to each kid, then one more to each. Each kid gets 2 balloons.

items.narration: Pat has 12 peaches. He packs them equally in 3 baskets. How many peaches are in each basket? Is it 3, 4, 5, or 6?
items.why: Share the peaches one at a time into 3 baskets. Each basket gets 4 peaches.

items.narration: Pat has 12 peaches. He puts 4 peaches in each basket. How many baskets does he fill?
items.why: Count by 4s. 4, 8, 12. That is 3 baskets.

items.narration: Nine grapes are shared equally by 3 kids. Move the frog to how many grapes each kid gets.
items.why: Share 9 grapes one at a time with 3 kids. Each kid gets 3 grapes.

items.narration: Ella has 12 cookies. She shares them equally with 6 friends. How many cookies does each friend get?
items.why: Give each of the 6 friends one cookie. Then give each friend one more. Each gets 2.

items.narration: Ava has 10 beads. She puts 5 beads in each bag. How many bags does she fill? Is it 3, 5, or 2?
items.why: Count by 5s. 5, 10. That makes 2 bags.

items.narration: Nia has 12 cookies. Who gets more cookies each: 2 friends sharing the 12, or 4 friends sharing the 12? Is it 2 friends or 4 friends?
items.why: 12 ÷ 2 = 6, but 12 ÷ 4 = 3. Fewer friends means bigger shares.

items.narration: Leo has 12 stars. He puts 2 stars in each group. How many groups does he make?
items.why: Count by 2s up to 12. 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12. That is 6 groups.

items.narration: Twelve muffins go into bags. Each bag holds 4 muffins. Move the frog to how many bags Mia fills.
items.why: Count by 4s. 4, 8, 12. That is 3 bags.

items.narration: We know 4 groups of 3 make 12. Now share 12 things equally into 4 groups. How many are in each group?
items.why: 4 groups of 3 make 12. So 12 shared into 4 groups gives 3 each.

items.narration: Kim has 9 plums. She gives 3 plums to each friend. How many friends get plums? Is it 3, 2, or 4?
items.why: Count by 3s. 3, 6, 9. That is 3 friends.

items.narration: What number is 4 hundreds, 5 tens, and 2 ones? Is it 452, 425, 542, or 245?
items.why: Hundreds go first, then tens, then ones. 4 hundreds is 400, 5 tens is 50, and 2 ones is 2. That makes 452.

items.narration: Maya has 300 + 40 + 6 stickers. What number is that?
items.why: Add the hundreds, tens, and ones. 300 plus 40 is 340, and 6 more makes 346.

items.narration: Move the frog to 700 on the number line.
items.why: The line counts by hundreds. Count 100, 200, 300, 400, 500, 600, 700. Seven hops of 100 get you there.

items.narration: Which number is seven hundred twenty-one? Is it 721, 712, 127, or 701?
items.why: Seven hundred is 700. Twenty-one is 20 and 1. Put them together to get 721.

items.narration: Each star is a sheet of 100 stickers. Maya has these sheets. How many stickers is that in all?
items.why: There are 6 sheets, and each one is 100. 6 hundreds is 600.
There are no tens, so the tens place holds a 0. 8 hundreds and 6 ones make 806.

items.narration: Type the number with 9 hundreds, 0 tens, and 4 ones.
items.why: 9 hundreds is 900. There are no tens, and 4 ones. So the number is 904.

items.narration: Move the frog to 350 on the number line.
items.why: 350 is halfway between 300 and 400. Count by 50s from 300 to land on 350.

items.narration: In the number 583, what is the 8 worth? Is it 8, 80, or 800?
items.why: The 8 is in the tens place. 8 tens is 80.

items.narration: A number has 2 hundreds, 3 tens, and some ones. The number is 238. How many ones does it have?
items.why: 200 plus 30 is 230. To reach 238, you need 8 more. So there are 8 ones.

items.narration: Jay has 3 sheets of 100 stickers and 14 strips of 10 stickers. How many stickers does he have?
items.why: 14 strips of 10 is 140. Add the 3 sheets, which is 300. 300 plus 140 makes 440.

items.narration: Move the frog to six hundred twenty-five on the number line.
items.why: Six hundred twenty-five is 600 and 25. Go to 600, then hop one more step of 25.

items.narration: Which number is 6 hundreds and 15 tens? Is it 750, 615, 651, or 156?
items.why: 15 tens is 150. Add 600 and 150 to get 750.

items.narration: Which way builds 360? Is it 300 + 60, 300 + 6, 30 + 60, or 3 + 60?
items.why: 360 is 3 hundreds and 6 tens. That is 300 plus 60.

items.narration: Move the frog to nine hundred fifty on the number line.
items.why: Nine hundred fifty is 900 and 50. It sits halfway between 900 and 1000.

items.narration: In the number 352, what is the 3 worth? Is it 3, 30, or 300?
items.why: The 3 is in the hundreds place. That means 3 hundreds, which is 300.

items.narration: Maya has 4 hundreds, 2 tens, and 6 ones. What number is that?
items.why: 4 hundreds is 400. 2 tens is 20. 6 ones is 6. Put them together to get 426.

items.narration: Move the frog to 5 hundreds.
items.why: One hundred is 100. Five hundreds is 100 five times, which is 500.

items.narration: In the number 84, what is the 8 worth? Is it 8, 80, or 800?
items.why: The 8 is in the tens place. That means 8 tens, which is 80.

items.narration: What digit is in the tens place of 639?
items.why: The tens place is the middle digit. In 639, the middle digit is 3, so there are 3 tens.

items.narration: Omar has 507 cards. What does the zero in 507 do? It makes the number bigger, it is worth 7, or it holds the tens place?
items.why: The zero shows there are no tens. It holds the tens place so the 5 stays in the hundreds place.

items.narration: In the number 862, what is the 6 worth?
items.why: The 6 is in the tens place. That means 6 tens, which is 60.

items.narration: Move the frog to the number with 6 hundreds and 5 tens.
items.why: 6 hundreds is 600. 5 tens is 50. Together that makes 650.

items.narration: Which number has a 4 in the hundreds place? Is it 342, 423, or 234?
items.why: The hundreds place is the first digit. In 423 the first digit is 4, so it has 4 hundreds.

items.narration: Tom has 8 hundreds, 0 tens, and 5 ones. What number is that?
items.why: 8 hundreds is 800. There are no tens. 5 ones is 5. The zero holds the tens place, so the number is 805.

items.narration: Which 5 is worth more, the 5 in 358 or the 5 in 583?
items.why: In 358 the 5 is in the tens place, so it is 50. In 583 the 5 is in the hundreds place, so it is 500.

items.narration: 10 tens make one hundred. How many tens are in 300?
items.why: Each hundred is 10 tens. 300 is 3 hundreds, so it is 3 times 10 tens, which is 30 tens.

items.narration: Move the frog to the number with 3 hundreds, 7 tens, and 0 ones.
items.why: 3 hundreds is 300. 7 tens is 70. The zero ones add nothing. So the number is 370.

items.narration: The 3 in 30 is worth 30. The 3 in 300 is worth 300. How many times as much is 300 as 30? Is it 3, 10, or 100 times?
items.why: Each place is ten times bigger than the place next to it. 30 is 3 tens and 300 is 30 tens, so it is 10 times as much.

items.narration: A number has 2 hundreds, 14 tens, and 3 ones. What number is it?
items.why: 2 hundreds is 200. 14 tens is 140. 3 ones is 3. Add 200, 140, and 3 to get 343.

items.narration: Which is greater, 430 or 340?
items.why: Look at the hundreds first. 430 has 4 hundreds and 340 has 3 hundreds. So 430 is greater.

items.narration: Which is less, 520 or 250?
items.why: Compare the hundreds. 250 has 2 hundreds and 520 has 5 hundreds. So 250 is less.

items.narration: Sam has 275 points, Maya has 90 points, and Lena has 410 points. What is the greatest number of points?
items.why: 410 has 4 hundreds. 275 has 2 hundreds and 90 has none. So 410 is the greatest.

items.narration: Move the frog to 700.
Move the frog to 250.
items.why: This line goes from 200 to 300 by tens. 250 is halfway between 200 and 300.

items.narration: Which is greater, 583 or 538?
items.why: Both have 5 hundreds. Compare the tens. 8 tens is more than 3 tens, so 583 is greater.

items.narration: Maya has 462 stickers. Is 462 greater than 500 or less than 500?
items.why: 462 has 4 hundreds. 500 has 5 hundreds. So 462 is less than 500.

items.narration: Put 640, 604, and 460 in order from least to greatest. What is the middle number?
items.why: The order is 460, 604, 640. The number in the middle is 604.

items.narration: Move the frog to the number with 6 hundreds, 5 tens, and 0 ones.
items.why: 6 hundreds is 600. 5 tens is 50. Put them together to get 650.

items.narration: Which number is least: 705, 750, or 570?
items.why: 570 has 5 hundreds. The other two have 7 hundreds. So 570 is the least.

items.narration: Which number is greatest: 899, 989, 898, or 998?
items.why: All have 8 or 9 hundreds. 989 and 998 have 9 hundreds. Then 9 tens beats 8 tens, so 998 is greatest.

items.narration: Put 372, 327, 732, and 237 in order from greatest to least. What number is second?
items.why: The order from greatest is 732, 372, 327, 237. The second number is 372.

items.narration: Sam has 468 stickers. Maya has more than Sam but fewer than 470. How many stickers does Maya have?
items.why: The number right after 468 is 469. It is more than 468 and less than 470.

items.narration: Move the frog to the number that is 100 less than 875.
items.why: 100 less means one fewer hundred. 875 becomes 775.

items.narration: Which number is between 640 and 680: 630, 655, 690, or 710?
items.why: The number must be more than 640 and less than 680. Only 655 fits.

items.narration: Mia has 12 grapes. She shares them fairly between 2 friends. How many grapes does each friend get?
items.why: Hand out grapes one at a time to each friend. Both friends end up with 6 grapes.

items.narration: Leo has 9 stickers. He shares them fairly among 3 friends. How many stickers does each friend get? Is it 2, 3, 4, or 6?
items.why: Give each friend one sticker at a time. After 3 rounds, all 9 are gone. Each friend gets 3.

items.narration: Ava has 10 marbles. She shares them fairly among 5 friends. Move the frog to how many marbles each friend gets.
items.why: Make 5 equal groups from 10 marbles. Each group has 2 marbles.

items.narration: A pizza is cut into 4 equal slices. The picture shows one slice. What fraction of the pizza is one slice? Is it 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, or 1/5?
items.why: The pizza has 4 equal slices. One slice out of 4 is 1/4.

items.narration: Zoe has 16 apples. She shares them fairly among 4 friends. How many apples does each friend get?
items.why: Make 4 equal groups from 16 apples. Each group has 4 apples.

items.narration: A coach has 18 water bottles. She shares them fairly among 6 players. Move the frog to how many bottles each player gets.
items.why: Make 6 equal groups from 18 bottles. Each group has 3 bottles.

items.narration: Sam has 14 balls. He shares them fairly among 4 friends. Each friend gets whole balls and a part of a ball. How much does each friend get? Is it 3, 3 1/2, 4, or 2 1/2?
items.why: Each friend gets 3 balls, which uses 12. Two balls are left. Cut them into halves, so each friend gets one more half. That is 3 1/2.

items.narration: 5 friends each get 4 cards in a fair share. How many cards were there to share in all?
items.why: Five groups of 4 cards make all the cards. 5 × 4 = 20.

items.narration: Noah has 20 crackers. He shares them fairly among 4 friends. Move the frog to how many crackers each friend gets.
items.why: Make 4 equal groups from 20 crackers. Each group has 5 crackers.

items.narration: Lily has 12 stickers. She could share them among 3 friends, or among 4 friends. Which way gives each friend more? Is it 3 friends or 4 friends?
items.why: 12 shared by 3 gives 4 each. 12 shared by 4 gives 3 each. Fewer friends means a bigger share.

items.narration: Jay has 8 cookies. He shares them fairly among 3 friends. How much does each friend get? Is it 2 1/3, 2 2/3, 3, or 2 1/2?
items.why: Each friend gets 2 cookies, which uses 6. Two cookies are left. Cut each into thirds, so each friend gets 2 more thirds. That is 2 2/3.

items.narration: Kai has 17 cookies. He shares them fairly among 5 friends. Each friend gets 3 whole cookies. How many cookies are left over to cut?
items.why: Each of 5 friends gets 3, which uses 15 cookies. 17 take away 15 leaves 2.

items.narration: A bakery has 18 muffins. It shares them fairly between 2 stores. Move the frog to how many muffins each store gets.
items.why: Split 18 into 2 equal groups. Each group has 9 muffins.

items.narration: Ben has 5 sandwiches. He shares them fairly among 3 friends. How much does each friend get? Is it 1 1/3, 1 2/3, 2, or 1 1/2?
items.why: Each friend gets 1 sandwich, which uses 3. Two are left. Cut each into thirds, so each friend gets 2 more thirds. That is 1 2/3.

items.narration: 3 granola bars are shared fairly among 4 friends. Which picture shows one friend's share? Is it 1 of 4 parts picked, 2 of 3 parts picked, 3 of 8 parts picked, or 3 of 4 parts picked?
items.why: A bar cut into 4 equal parts with 3 picked is 3/4. The other pictures show different amounts.

items.narration: A pan is cut into 4 equal parts. 2 parts are picked. Which fraction is the same amount: 1/4, 3/4, or 1/2?
items.why: 2 of 4 equal parts is half of the pan. So 2/4 is the same amount as 1/2.

items.narration: A pizza is cut into 2 equal slices. Ana eats 1 slice, which is 1/2. If the pizza was cut into 4 equal slices, how many slices is the same amount?
items.why: Cutting each half in two makes 4 slices. Half of 4 slices is 2 slices.

items.narration: A pan is cut into 4 equal pieces. How many pieces make 1/2 of the pan? Move the frog to that number.
items.why: Half of 4 pieces is 2 pieces. So 2/4 is the same as 1/2.

items.narration: A pizza is cut into 10 equal slices. 2 slices are picked. Is that the same as 1/10, 1/5, or 2/5?
items.why: Cut into 5 big slices, each one covers 2 small slices. So 2/10 is the same as 1/5.

items.narration: A pan has 4 equal parts. 2 parts are picked. Is that the same amount as 1/2 of the pan? Yes or no?
items.why: 2 out of 4 equal parts is half the pan. So yes, they are the same amount.

items.narration: A circle is cut into 8 equal parts. 4 parts are picked. That is the same as 1/2. 1/2 equals how many eighths?
items.why: Eight parts split into two equal groups makes 4 in each group. So 1/2 is 4/8.

items.narration: 1/5 of a flatbread is the same as 2/10. Now Kai eats 3/5 of the flatbread. How many tenths is that? Move the frog to that number.
items.why: Each fifth is 2 tenths. Three fifths is 3 groups of 2, which is 6 tenths.

items.narration: A circle is cut into 3 equal parts. 2 parts are picked. Which is the same amount: 3/6, 2/6, or 4/6?
items.why: Cut each third into 2 sixths. Two thirds become 4 sixths.

items.narration: Which picture is the same amount as 1/2 of a circle? Is it 1/4 of the circle, 2/4 of the circle, 3/8 of the circle, or 2/6 of the circle?
items.why: Half of 4 equal parts is 2 parts. So 2/4 of the circle is the same as 1/2.

items.narration: A chocolate bar has 10 equal pieces. Zoe eats 4 pieces, which is 4/10. That is the same as how many fifths?
items.why: Two tenths make one fifth. Four tenths make 2 fifths.

items.narration: Sam ate 1/2 of a pan. Jo ate 4/8. Kit ate 3/6. Lee ate 2/5. The pans are the same size. Who ate a different amount from the others: Sam, Jo, Kit, or Lee?
items.why: 1/2, 4/8, and 3/6 are all half. Lee's 2/5 is less than half, so Lee is different.

items.narration: A pizza is cut into 6 equal slices. Mia eats 4 slices. Another pizza of the same size is cut into thirds. Mia's amount is how many thirds?
items.why: Two sixths make one third. Four sixths make 2 thirds.

items.narration: Dev ate 3/4 of a pan. If the pan was cut into 8 equal pieces, how many pieces did he eat? Move the frog to that number.
items.why: Each fourth is 2 eighths. Three fourths is 3 groups of 2, which is 6 eighths.

items.narration: 2 friends share 1 flatbread fairly. It is cut into 10 equal slices. Each friend gets 1/2. How many tenths does each friend get: 2, 5, 10, or 8?
items.why: Share 10 slices between 2 friends. Each friend gets 5 slices, so 1/2 is 5/10.

items.narration: 4 friends share 1 pan of brownies fairly. Each gets 1/4. The pan is cut into 8 equal pieces instead. How many pieces does each friend get?
items.why: Share 8 pieces between 4 friends. Each friend gets 2 pieces, so 1/4 is 2/8.

items.narration: An array has 2 rows. Each row has 5 dots. How many dots are there in all?
items.why: Count by fives for 2 rows: 5, 10. So 2 × 5 = 10.

items.narration: An array has 3 rows with 4 dots in each row. How many dots in all? Is it 7, 12, 10, or 15?
items.why: Count by fours 3 times: 4, 8, 12. So 3 × 4 = 12.

items.narration: Sam makes an array with 2 rows of 6 stickers. Move the frog to the number of stickers in all.
items.why: Two rows of 6 is 6 + 6. That makes 12 stickers.

items.narration: Ana puts 10 stickers in 2 equal rows. How many stickers are in each row? Is it 8, 12, 4, or 5?
items.why: Share 10 into 2 equal rows. Each row gets 5, because 2 × 5 = 10.

items.narration: An array has 12 dots. There are 4 dots in each row. How many rows are there?
items.why: Count by fours until you reach 12: 4, 8, 12. That took 3 rows.

items.narration: A hockey team lines up in an array. There are 6 rows with 7 players in each row. How many players in all?
items.why: Count by sevens 6 times: 7, 14, 21, 28, 35, 42. So 6 × 7 = 42.

items.narration: A tray has 4 rows of muffins with 8 in each row. Which fact finds how many muffins in all? Is it 4 + 8, 8 ÷ 4, or 4 × 8?
items.why: Equal rows use multiplying. 4 rows of 8 is 4 × 8, which is 32 muffins.

items.narration: There are 35 cards in an array. Each row has 5 cards. Move the frog to the number of rows.
items.why: Think 5 times what is 35. Counting by fives, 5 × 7 = 35, so there are 7 rows.

items.narration: Leo lines up 24 counters in 6 equal rows. How many counters are in each row? Is it 3, 6, 4, or 18?
items.why: Think 6 times what is 24. Since 6 × 4 = 24, each row has 4.

items.narration: A garden has 9 rows of plants. Each row has 5 plants. How many plants are in the garden?
A game board is an array with 9 rows and 8 columns. How many squares are on the board?
items.why: Use 10 × 8 = 80, then take away one row of 8. 80 minus 8 is 72.

items.narration: A big array has 10 rows. Each row has 7 dots. Move the frog to the number of dots in all.
items.why: Each row adds 7 more. Ten rows of 7 is 70, because 10 × 7 is 7 tens.

items.narration: Zoe knows 5 × 8 is 40. Now she adds one more row of 8 to make 6 rows. What is 6 × 8? Is it 48, 40, 45, or 56?
items.why: Start with 5 rows of 8, which is 40. One more row adds 8. So 40 + 8 = 48.

items.narration: A big array has 100 dots. Each row has 10 dots. Move the frog to the number of rows.
items.why: Think 10 times what is 100. Since 10 × 10 = 100, there are 10 rows.

items.narration: A seating chart is an array with 7 rows and 8 seats in each row. Move the frog to the number of seats in all.
items.why: Count by eights 7 times: 8, 16, 24, 32, 40, 48, 56. So 7 × 8 = 56.

items.narration: What is 2 × 5? Is it 7, 10, or 12?
items.why: 2 groups of 5 is 5 and 5 more. 5 + 5 = 10.

items.narration: What is 3 × 10?
items.why: Count by 10s three times. 10, 20, 30. So 3 × 10 = 30.

items.narration: Count by 2s to find 4 × 2. Move the frog to that number.
items.why: Skip count by 2s four times. 2, 4, 6, 8. So 4 × 2 = 8.

items.narration: Maya shares these 10 cookies equally between 2 friends. How many cookies does each friend get?
items.why: Think 2 times what is 10? 5 × 2 = 10, so each friend gets 5.

items.narration: What is 20 ÷ 10? Is it 2, 10, or 30?
items.why: Count by 10s. 10, 20. That takes 2 jumps, so 20 ÷ 10 = 2.

items.narration: What is 7 × 5? Is it 30, 35, 40, or 45?
items.why: Count by 5s seven times. 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35. So 7 × 5 = 35.

items.narration: Jay has 8 pairs of socks. Each pair has 2 socks. How many socks is that in all?
items.why: Double 8. 8 + 8 = 16. So 8 × 2 = 16 socks.

items.narration: Count by 5s to find 7 × 5. Move the frog to that number.
items.why: Hop by 5s seven times. 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35. The frog lands on 35.

items.narration: A hockey coach has 40 pucks. She puts 5 pucks in each bucket. How many buckets does she fill?
items.why: Think 5 times what is 40? Count by 5s to 40. That is 8 jumps, so 40 ÷ 5 = 8.

items.narration: Leo shares 18 stickers equally between 2 friends. How many stickers does each friend get? Is it 8, 9, 16, or 20?
items.why: Think 2 times what is 18? Double 9 is 18, so 9 × 2 = 18 and 18 ÷ 2 = 9.

items.narration: 9 kids on a team each score 5 points. How many points did the team score in all?
Find 45 ÷ 5. Think 5 times what is 45? Move the frog to that number.
items.why: Count by 5s until you reach 45. 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40, 45. That is 9 jumps.

items.narration: What number times 5 makes 35? Is it 6, 7, 8, or 9?
items.why: Count by 5s to 35. 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35. That is 7 jumps, so 7 × 5 = 35.

items.narration: What number times 10 makes 80?
A coach packs 6 boxes. Each box has 10 stars. Move the frog to the total number of stars.
items.why: Count by 10s six times. 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60. So there are 60 stars.

items.narration: 3 × 5 is the same as 5 × what number? Is it 5, 8, 3, or 15?
items.why: You can multiply in any order. 3 × 5 and 5 × 3 both make 15.

items.narration: Mia knows 6 × 2 = 12. So what is 2 × 6?
items.why: Swapping the order does not change the answer. 2 × 6 is the same as 6 × 2, which is 12.

items.narration: Move the frog to the answer of 4 × 2.
items.why: 4 groups of 2 is 2 + 2 + 2 + 2. That makes 8.

items.narration: 12 ÷ 3 = 4. Which fact checks it? Is it 4 + 3 = 7, or 4 × 3 = 12?
items.why: Multiply the answer by the number you divided by. 4 × 3 = 12, so it matches.

items.narration: Here are 10 apples. Mia shares them equally into 2 baskets. How many apples are in each basket?
items.why: Think 2 times what is 10. 2 × 5 = 10, so each basket gets 5.

items.narration: 4 × 6 is the same as 4 × 5 plus 4 times what number? Is it 2, 4, 6, or 1?
items.why: Split 6 into 5 and 1. So 4 × 6 is 4 × 5 plus 4 × 1.

items.narration: Sam knows 3 × 5 = 15. He adds one more group of 3. What is 3 × 6?
items.why: 3 × 6 is 3 × 5 plus one more 3. 15 + 3 = 18.

items.narration: Move the frog to the answer of 5 × 7.
items.why: Swap to 7 × 5. Count by 5s seven times: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35.

items.narration: 24 cookies are shared equally onto 4 trays. Think 4 times what number is 24. How many cookies are on each tray?
items.why: Use multiplying to divide. 4 × 6 = 24, so 24 ÷ 4 = 6.

items.narration: 6 × 3 = 18. Which division fact goes with it? Is it 18 ÷ 3 = 6, 18 ÷ 6 = 6, or 18 ÷ 3 = 3?
items.why: If 6 groups of 3 make 18, then 18 split into groups of 3 gives 6. So 18 ÷ 3 = 6.

items.narration: Lena wants 8 × 7. She uses 8 × 5 = 40 and 8 × 2 = 16. Add the two parts. What is 8 × 7?
items.why: Split 7 into 5 and 2. Then 40 + 16 = 56.

items.narration: Move the frog to the answer of 36 ÷ 4. Think 4 times what number is 36.
Ben thinks 42 ÷ 6 = 8. He checks with 8 × 6 = 48. Is Ben right? Yes or no?
items.why: Multiplying checks dividing. 8 × 6 is 48, not 42, so Ben is not right. The answer is 7.

items.narration: Zoe wants 6 × 9. She splits 9 into 5 and 4. 6 × 5 = 30 and 6 × 4 = 24. What is 6 × 9?
items.why: Add the two parts: 30 + 24 = 54. So 6 × 9 = 54.

items.narration: Which one is the same as 7 × 6? Is it 7 × 5 + 1, 6 × 5 + 7, or 7 × 5 + 7?
items.why: Split 6 into 5 and 1. So 7 × 6 is 7 × 5 plus 7 × 1, which is 35 + 7 = 42.

items.narration: Ana has 4 bags. Each bag has 3 apples. How many apples does she have in all? Is it 7, 9, 12, or 15?
items.why: 4 bags with 3 apples each is 4 groups of 3. Count by threes: 3, 6, 9, 12.

items.narration: Here are 12 cookies. Mia shares them equally among 3 friends. How many cookies does each friend get? Is it 4, 3, 9, or 36?
items.why: Share the cookies one at a time to 3 friends. Each friend gets 4.

items.narration: Sam makes 5 hops of 4 on a number line. Which number sentence matches? Is it 5 + 4, 5 × 4, or 4 ÷ 5?
items.why: Equal hops are equal groups. 5 hops of 4 means 5 groups of 4, so multiply: 5 × 4.

items.narration: Tom has 20 marbles. He puts 5 marbles in each bag. How many bags does he fill? Is it 15, 25, 5, or 4?
items.why: Make groups of 5 from 20. Hop back by 5 from 20 and count the hops. There are 4.

items.narration: Dan makes 8 batches of muffins. Each batch needs 1/4 cup of milk. How many cups of milk does he use in all? Is it 1, 2, 4, or 8?
items.why: Four hops of 1/4 make 1. So 8 hops of 1/4 make 2 cups.

items.narration: There are 3 boxes. Each box has 5 pencils. How many pencils are there in all?
items.why: 3 groups of 5 is 5, 10, 15. There are 15 pencils.

items.narration: Eli has 24 stickers. He shares them equally among 6 friends. How many stickers does each friend get?
items.why: Think of 6 times what is 24. Since 6 × 4 = 24, each friend gets 4.

items.narration: A team has 8 players. There are 56 players in all. How many teams are there?
items.why: Count how many groups of 8 fit in 56. Since 8 × 7 = 56, there are 7 teams.

items.narration: A frog hops 1/3 each time, starting at 0. How many hops does it take to reach 2?
items.why: It takes 3 hops of 1/3 to reach 1. To reach 2, it takes 3 more. That is 6 hops.

items.narration: Mia fills 10 glasses. Each glass gets 1/2 cup of juice. How many cups of juice does she use?
items.why: Two glasses use 1 cup. 10 glasses make 5 pairs, so she uses 5 cups.

items.narration: The frog starts at 0. It makes 4 hops of 3. Drag the frog to where it lands.
items.why: Hop by 3 four times: 3, 6, 9, 12. The frog lands on 12.

items.narration: The frog starts at 0. It makes 5 hops of 2. Drag the frog to where it lands.
items.why: Hop by 2 five times: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. The frog lands on 10.

items.narration: The frog starts at 30. It hops back 5 each time. It makes 4 hops back. Drag the frog to where it lands.
items.why: Hop back by 5 four times: 25, 20, 15, 10. The frog lands on 10.

items.narration: The frog starts at 0. It makes 6 hops of 1/2. Drag the frog to where it lands.
items.why: Two hops of 1/2 make 1. Six hops make 3 groups of 1, so the frog lands on 3.

items.narration: The frog starts at 4. It hops back 1/2 each time. It makes 4 hops back. Drag the frog to where it lands.
items.why: Two hops of 1/2 make 1. Four hops back make 2, so the frog lands on 2.

items.narration: A pizza is cut into 4 equal slices. Mia eats 3 slices. What fraction of the pizza did she eat? Is it 1/4, 3/4, or 4/4?
items.why: Each slice is one fourth. Mia ate 3 slices, so that is 3 fourths, or 3/4.

items.narration: This bar is cut into 5 equal pieces. 3 pieces are picked. One fifth plus one fifth plus one fifth is how many fifths?
items.why: Count the picked pieces. There are 3, so you have 3 fifths.

items.narration: Jo eats one eighth of a pan of brownies at each bite. Move the frog to how many eighths Jo has eaten after 5 bites.
items.why: Each bite adds one eighth. After 5 bites, Jo has 5 eighths.

items.narration: Look at the fraction 2/5. What does the top number, 2, count? Is it how big each piece is, how many bars, or how many pieces?
items.prompt: What does the top number count?
items.why: The top number counts the pieces. The bottom number tells how big each piece is.

items.narration: A circle is cut into 8 equal parts. 3 parts are picked. That is 3/8. What is the bottom number?
items.why: The bottom number tells how many equal parts make the whole. This circle has 8 parts.

items.narration: Add one fifth three times. What fraction do you get? Is it 3/5, 5/3, 1/5, or 3/3?
items.why: Each piece is one fifth, so the bottom number is 5. You have 3 pieces, so the top number is 3. That makes 3/5.

items.narration: This strip has 8 equal parts. 5 parts are picked. You add one eighth again and again to make 5/8. How many times do you add it?
items.why: The top number counts the pieces. In 5/8, there are 5 pieces of one eighth, so you add it 5 times.

items.narration: The frog hops one tenth each time. How many hops does it take to reach 7/10? Move the frog to that number of hops.
items.why: Each hop is one tenth. To get 7 tenths, the frog needs 7 hops.

items.narration: A pizza is cut into 6 equal slices. 4 slices are picked. Which addition matches the picked part? Is it 1/6 + 1/6, 1/6 + 1/6 + 1/6, 1/6 + 1/6 + 1/6 + 1/6, or 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4?
items.prompt: Which sum matches the picked part?
items.why: Each slice is one sixth. 4 slices means adding one sixth four times, which is 4/6.

items.narration: Kai eats 2 eighths of a pan of brownies. Then he eats 3 more eighths. How many eighths has he eaten in all?
items.why: Each piece is one eighth. Count all the pieces: 2 and 3 more make 5 eighths.

items.narration: Ana takes 4 pieces of one sixth. Ben takes 4 pieces of one eighth. Cy takes 4 pieces of one tenth. Whose share is the biggest? Is it 4/10, 4/6, or 4/8?
items.why: All three have 4 pieces. Sixths are bigger pieces than eighths or tenths. So 4/6 is the biggest.

items.narration: There are 2 chocolate bars, each cut into 4 equal pieces. 6 pieces are picked. That is 6/4. One fourth is added how many times?
items.why: The top number counts the pieces. In 6/4 there are 6 pieces of one fourth, so you add it 6 times.

items.narration: One whole is 3 thirds. How many thirds make 2 wholes? Move the frog to that number.
items.why: One whole is 3 thirds. Two wholes is 3 + 3, which is 6 thirds.

items.narration: Sam thinks 5/6 is 5 pieces, and each piece is one sixth. Maya thinks 5/6 is 6 pieces, and each piece is one fifth. Who is right? Is it Sam or Maya?
items.why: The bottom number, 6, gives the piece size, one sixth. The top number, 5, counts the pieces. So Sam is right.

items.narration: Dev adds one twelfth 12 times. This fills a whole bar. How many wholes does he have?
items.why: 12 pieces of one twelfth is 12/12. That fills the bar once, so it is 1 whole.

items.narration: A pizza is cut into 4 equal slices. Mia eats 3 of them. What fraction of the pizza did she eat? Is it 3/4, 1/4, or 4/4?
items.why: The pizza has 4 equal slices, so the bottom number is 4. Mia ate 3 slices, so the top number is 3. That is 3/4.

items.narration: A pizza is cut into 6 equal slices. Two slices are picked. How many equal slices make the whole pizza?
