items.narration: A pizza is cut into 6 equal slices. 5 sixths of it are still there. Ben eats 2 sixths. How much is left now? Is it 3/6, 7/6, 3/12, or 2/6?
items.why: Take away the pieces: 5 sixths minus 2 sixths is 3 sixths. The slices are the same size, so the denominator stays 6.

items.narration: 1 fifth plus 3 fifths equals how many fifths?
items.why: The units are both fifths. Add the counts: 1 + 3 = 4, so the answer is 4 fifths.

items.narration: A chocolate bar is cut into 10 equal pieces. The picture shows 7 tenths left. Lena eats 4 tenths. How many tenths are left?
items.why: Start with 7 pieces and take away 4. That leaves 3 pieces, so 3 tenths are left.

items.narration: The number line goes from 0 to 1 in steps of one fourth, or 0.25. Move the frog to 1/4 + 2/4.
items.why: 1 fourth plus 2 fourths is 3 fourths. Count 3 steps of one fourth from 0 to land on 0.75.

items.narration: Priya runs 4/9 of a kilometre, then 7/9 of a kilometre. How far does she run in total? Is it 3/9, 28/9, 11/9, or 11/18?
items.why: Add the numerators: 4 + 7 = 11. The denominator stays 9, so she runs 11/9 of a kilometre.

items.narration: A recipe uses 3/8 cup of sugar in the batter and 7/8 cup in the icing. The total is how many eighths of a cup?
items.why: Both amounts are counted in eighths. Add 3 + 7 = 10, so the total is 10 eighths of a cup.

items.narration: The number line goes from 0 to 2 in steps of one fourth, or 0.25. Move the frog to 7/4 - 3/4.
items.why: 7 fourths take away 3 fourths leaves 4 fourths. That is one whole, so the frog lands on 1.

items.narration: Is 5/6 + 4/6 greater than 1 whole? Yes or no?
items.why: 5 sixths plus 4 sixths is 9 sixths. One whole is 6 sixths, and 9 is more than 6, so the answer is yes.

items.narration: The number line goes from 0 to 2 in steps of one fourth, or 0.25. Move the frog to 1/4 + 5/4.
items.why: 1 fourth plus 5 fourths is 6 fourths. Count 6 steps of one fourth from 0 to land on 1.5.

items.narration: Maya ate 5/12 of a pan of brownies on Friday and 4/12 on Saturday. What fraction of the whole pan is left? Is it 9/12, 9/24, 1/12, or 3/12?
items.why: She ate 5 + 4 = 9 twelfths. The whole pan is 12 twelfths, so 12 minus 9 leaves 3 twelfths.

items.narration: In a relay, Zoe runs 5/8 of a kilometre, Omar runs 7/8, and Lee runs 4/8. What is the total distance in kilometres?
items.why: Add the numerators: 5 + 7 + 4 = 16, so the total is 16 eighths. Since 8 eighths make one whole, 16 eighths make 2.

items.narration: Sam has 2 cups of flour. Cut into sixths, that is 12 sixths. He uses 5 sixths. How many sixths of a cup are left?
items.why: Two cups is 12 sixths. Take away 5 sixths: 12 - 5 = 7, so 7 sixths of a cup are left.

items.narration: The number line goes from 0 to 3 in steps of one fourth, or 0.25. Move the frog to 1 3/4 + 3/4.
items.why: 1 3/4 is 7 fourths. Add 3 fourths to get 10 fourths, which is 2 and 2 fourths, or 2.5.

items.narration: The number line goes from 0 to 3 in steps of one fourth, or 0.25. Move the frog to 2 1/4 - 6/4.
items.why: 2 1/4 is 9 fourths. Take away 6 fourths to leave 3 fourths, which is 0.75.

items.narration: Priya adds four scoops of 1/3 cup. What is 4 × 1/3? Is it 4/3, 3/4, or 1/12?
items.why: 4 × 1/3 means four one-thirds added together. Add the numerators, 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 4, and keep the denominator 3. That gives 4/3.

items.narration: A scoop holds 1/4 cup. How many scoops does it take to fill 1 whole cup?
items.why: The denominator 4 tells us that 4 fourths make one whole. So it takes 4 scoops to fill 1 cup.

items.narration: Move the frog to 3 × 1/2. The line goes from 0 to 3 in steps of one half. Labels show decimals, so one half is 0.5.
items.why: 3 × 1/2 means three halves. Hop by one half three times: 0.5, 1, then 1.5.

items.narration: 2 × 1/5 equals how many fifths? Type the numerator.
items.why: 2 × 1/5 is two one-fifths added together. That makes 2 fifths, or 2/5, so the numerator is 2.

items.narration: How many halves fit in 2 wholes? Is it 1, 2, 3, or 4?
items.why: Each whole holds 2 halves. Two wholes hold 2 × 2, which is 4 halves.

items.narration: A trail mix scoop holds 1/3 cup. How many scoops does it take to fill 4 cups? Find 4 ÷ 1/3.
items.why: One cup takes 3 scoops. Four cups take four times as many, so 4 × 3 = 12 scoops.

items.narration: Marcus runs 1/4 kilometre each lap. He runs 5 laps. What is 5 × 1/4? Is it 1/20, 4/5, or 5/4?
items.why: Five laps of one fourth is five fourths. Add the numerators, 5 ones, and keep the denominator 4. The answer is 5/4 kilometres.

items.narration: Move the frog to 5 ÷ 1/2. That is how many halves fit in 5 wholes. The line goes from 0 to 10.
items.why: Each whole has 2 halves. Five wholes have 5 × 2 = 10 halves.

items.narration: A bottle cap holds 1/5 of a cup of water. How many caps does it take to fill 3 cups? Find 3 ÷ 1/5.
items.why: One cup holds 5 fifths. Three cups hold 3 × 5, which is 15 caps.

items.narration: Which is greater, 4 × 1/5 or 4 ÷ 1/5?
items.why: 4 × 1/5 is only 4/5, less than one whole. 4 ÷ 1/5 asks how many fifths fit in 4 wholes, and that is 4 × 5 = 20.

items.narration: A chef pours soup with a ladle that holds 1/4 litre. How many ladles does it take to fill a pot with 8 litres? Find 8 ÷ 1/4.
items.why: One litre needs 4 ladles. Eight litres need 8 × 4, which is 32 ladles.

items.narration: Move the frog to 7 × 1/4. The line goes from 0 to 3 in steps of one fourth. Labels show decimals, so one fourth is 0.25.
items.why: 7 × 1/4 is seven fourths. Seven steps of 0.25 land on 1.75, which is 1 3/4.

items.narration: A jug holds 6 litres. Maya fills it using a cup that holds 1/4 litre. How many cups does she pour? Is it 2, 10, 24, or 12?
items.why: Each litre takes 4 cups. Six litres take 6 × 4, which is 24 cups.

items.narration: Nine halves is the same as 9 × 1/2. Type the answer as a decimal.
items.why: Nine halves is 9/2. Two halves make one whole, so 9 halves make 4 wholes and one half left over, which is 4.5.

items.narration: True or false. 5 ÷ 1/8 equals 40.
items.why: One whole holds 8 eighths. Five wholes hold 5 × 8, which is 40. So the statement is true.

items.narration: Mia wants to make a boat. What does she do first: plan, test, or make it better?
items.why: Mia plans first. She thinks about what to use before she builds anything.

items.narration: Mia uses tape and a foam tray to put her boat together. Which step is that: plan, build, or test?
items.why: Putting the pieces together is the build step. Mia makes her boat.

items.narration: Mia puts her boat in water to see if it floats. Which step is that: build, test, or plan?
items.why: Trying it out is the test step. Mia sees if her boat floats.

items.narration: True or false: We test a thing to see if it works.
items.why: That is true. A test shows us if our thing works well.

items.narration: Which one is the odd one out: plan, build, test, or nap?
items.why: Plan, build, and test are steps for making things. A nap is not a step.

items.narration: Mia has built her boat. What step comes next: plan, test, or buy a toy?
items.why: After we build, we test. Testing shows if the boat floats.

items.narration: Mia's boat tipped over in the test. What should she do: make it better, or throw it away?
items.why: We can fix a problem. Mia makes her boat better, then tests it again.

items.narration: Which one is part of the plan step: think what to use, tape the pieces, or float it in water?
items.why: Planning means thinking before you start. Taping is building. Floating it is testing.

items.narration: Mia plans, builds, and tests. What step comes last: plan, build, or make it better?
items.why: After the test, we make it better. Then we can test again.

items.narration: Ben's tower fell down in a test. True or false: Ben can fix it and test again.
items.why: That is true. Fixing a problem and trying again is how we make things better.

items.narration: Sam's paper plane falls fast. What should he do: give up, hide it, or change it, test again?
items.why: A good maker changes the plane and tests again. Trying again helps us learn.

items.narration: Which list has the steps in the right order: plan, build, test; or test, plan, build; or build, test, plan?
items.why: We plan first, then build, then test. After that we can make it better.

items.narration: Why do we test something we made: to see if it works, to make it pretty, or to be done fast?
items.why: A test shows us what works and what does not. Then we know what to fix.

items.narration: Kai's cup holder tipped over. He gives it a wide base. Which step is the wide base: plan, test, or make it better?
items.why: After a test, we change the thing to fix it. That is make it better.

items.narration: True or false: We make it better before we test it the first time.
items.why: That is false. We build first and test it. The test shows us what to make better.

items.narration: Biscuit is a puppy. What does he need: water, or a toy?
items.why: Puppies are living things. All living things need water to stay alive.

items.narration: True or false: living things need air.
items.why: It is true. Animals and plants all need air to stay alive.

items.narration: Which one is a living thing: a dog, a rock, or a spoon?
items.why: A dog is alive. It eats, drinks, and grows. A rock and a spoon are not alive.

items.narration: Mia's bean plant wants to grow. What does it need: water, plastic, or a phone?
items.why: Plants need water to grow. Plastic and phones are not needs.

items.narration: Which one is a need for living things: food, or a game?
items.why: Living things must have food to stay alive. A game is fun, but it is not a need.

items.narration: Which one is not a need for living things: water, food, a bike, or air?
items.why: Water, food, and air are needs. A bike is fun, but living things do not need it.

items.narration: Mia puts her plant by a sunny window. What does the sun give: heat, a toy, or candy?
items.why: The sun gives heat. Living things need heat to stay warm and grow.

items.narration: True or false: only animals need water.
items.why: It is false. Plants need water too. All living things need water.

items.narration: A cow eats grass. Which need does the grass meet: food, space, or heat?
items.prompt: What need is grass for a cow?
items.why: Grass is the cow's food. Eating gives the cow power to live and grow.

items.narration: A bear sleeps in a den in winter. Which need does a den give: shelter, water, or air?
items.why: A den is a home. It gives the bear shelter from the cold and snow.

items.narration: Mia plants ten seeds in one tiny cup. They are squeezed. What do they need more of: space, candy, or toys?
items.why: Plants need space to grow. Seeds squeezed together do not have room.

items.narration: Biscuit has food, a warm bed, and air. What does he still need: water, a hat, or a toy?
items.why: Biscuit still needs water. A hat and a toy are not needs.

items.narration: True or false: a rock needs food.
items.why: It is false. A rock is not alive, so it has no needs. Living things need food.

items.narration: A plant sits in a freezer. Which need is it missing: heat, a hat, or a toy?
items.why: A freezer is very cold. The plant needs heat to grow well.

items.narration: Which group has only needs of living things: air, water, and food; toys, candy, and games; or hats, cars, and bikes?
items.why: Air, water, and food are needs. Toys, candy, games, hats, cars, and bikes are not needs.

items.narration: Roots help a plant get something from the soil. Is it water, or sunlight?
items.why: Roots drink water from the soil. Leaves are the parts that catch sunlight.

items.narration: A rabbit has soft fur. Fur helps the rabbit stay what: warm, or wet?
items.why: Fur keeps an animal warm. It is like a cozy coat.

items.narration: Which part helps a bird fly: wings, or roots?
items.why: Wings help a bird fly. Roots are plant parts that stay in the soil.

items.narration: True or false: Leaves help a plant use sunlight to make food.
items.why: That is true. Leaves catch sunlight, and the plant makes food with it.

items.narration: Which animal uses fins to swim: a dog, a cow, or a fish?
items.why: A fish has fins. Fins help it move through the water.

items.narration: A duck has webbed feet. What do they help the duck do: swim, or climb trees?
items.why: Webbed feet push against the water. They help a duck swim.

items.narration: Which plant part holds the plant in the soil: leaves, roots, or petals?
items.prompt: What holds a plant in place?
items.why: Roots grow into the soil. They hold the plant up so it does not fall.

items.narration: Which one is the odd one out. Which does not help an animal move: wings, legs, fins, or fur?
items.prompt: Which is the odd one out?
items.why: Wings, legs, and fins help animals move. Fur keeps an animal warm.

items.narration: A cactus has a thick stem that holds water. This helps it live in a place that is dry, or wet?
items.why: A cactus stores water in its stem. That helps it live where it is dry.

items.narration: A bird has a sharp beak. What does the beak help it do: eat food, or stay warm?
items.why: A bird uses its beak to pick up and eat food. Feathers help it stay warm.

items.narration: Which part helps an animal see food and danger: a tail, eyes, or fur?
items.why: Eyes let an animal see. Then it can find food and spot danger.

items.narration: A turtle has a hard shell. What does the shell help it do: stay safe, or fly?
items.why: A hard shell protects a turtle. The turtle can hide inside it from danger.

items.narration: Which one is not a plant part: roots, leaves, wings, or stem?
items.prompt: Which is not a plant part?
items.why: Roots, leaves, and stems are plant parts. Wings belong to animals like birds.

items.narration: True or false: A fish uses wings to swim.
items.why: That is false. A fish uses fins and its tail to swim. Wings are for flying.

items.narration: Some animals dig with big claws. Which one digs: a duck, a mole, or a fish?
items.why: A mole has strong claws. It digs tunnels in the soil to find food and hide.

items.narration: Which body part helps you see: your eyes, your ears, or your nose?
items.why: Your eyes help you see. Ears are for hearing and your nose is for smelling.

items.narration: Which body part helps you hear: your tongue, your ears, or your eyes?
items.why: Your ears help you hear sounds like music and voices.

items.narration: Your nose has a job. What does your nose do: smell, see, or hear?
items.why: Your nose helps you smell things, like flowers and bread.

items.narration: Your tongue has a job. What does your tongue do: taste, see, or hear?
items.why: Your tongue helps you taste. You can taste sweet, sour, and salty foods.

items.narration: True or false: Your skin helps you feel things, like soft or cold.
items.prompt: True or false: skin helps you feel.
items.why: It is true. Your skin helps you feel soft, hot, cold, and rough things.

items.narration: Mia smells cookies baking in the oven. Which body part does she use: her nose, her ears, or her eyes?
items.why: Mia uses her nose to smell. Noses pick up the smell of cookies.

items.narration: Where are your eyes: on your face, on your foot, or on your hand?
items.why: Your eyes are on your face, above your nose.

items.narration: Which is the odd one out: eyes, ears, nose, or knee? Three of them help us sense the world.
items.prompt: Which is the odd one out?
items.why: Eyes, ears, and nose help us sense things. A knee helps us bend our leg.

items.narration: Mia pets a soft kitten. Which body part feels the soft fur: her skin, her tongue, or her ears?
items.why: Skin helps us feel. Mia's hand skin feels the soft fur.

items.narration: Which body part covers your whole body: your skin, your nose, or your eyes?
items.why: Skin covers your whole body. It keeps your insides safe.

items.narration: A dog barks behind a closed door. Mia cannot see it. Which part helps her know? Her ears, her eyes, or her skin?
items.why: Mia hears the bark with her ears. She does not need to see the dog.

items.narration: True or false: You smell with your eyes.
items.prompt: True or false: you smell with your eyes.
items.why: It is false. You smell with your nose. Your eyes help you see.

items.narration: Which one is a job for your tongue: taste a lemon, hear a song, or see a rainbow?
items.prompt: What is a job for your tongue?
items.why: Your tongue tastes. A lemon tastes sour. Ears hear songs and eyes see rainbows.

items.narration: Which one is a nose: a nose, an ear, or an eye?
items.why: A nose sits in the middle of your face. It helps you smell.

items.narration: Mia closes her eyes. What can she still do: see her toys, hear a song, or see a rainbow?
items.why: With closed eyes, Mia cannot see. She can still hear a song with her ears.

items.narration: Which air is healthy to breathe: smoky air, or clean air?
items.why: Clean air is healthy. Living things need clean air to breathe.

items.narration: True or false: Fish need clean water to live.
items.why: This is true. Fish swim in water and breathe in it. Clean water keeps them well.

items.narration: A rabbit is hungry. Which one is good food for a rabbit: a rock, a carrot, or a plastic bag?
items.why: A carrot is good food for a rabbit. Rocks and plastic are not food.

items.narration: Which one does not belong in a healthy pond: clean water, fish, or trash?
items.why: Trash does not belong in a pond. Clean water and fish belong there.

items.narration: Which one needs clean air to live: a rock, a toy, or a bird?
items.why: A bird is a living thing. It needs clean air. Rocks and toys are not alive.

items.narration: A pond helps a frog get what it needs. What can a healthy pond give the frog: clean water, trash, or smoke?
items.prompt: What does a healthy pond give?
items.why: A healthy pond has clean water. The frog needs it to live and stay well.

items.narration: Mia sees trash in the pond. What can she do to help: pick up the trash, or drop more trash?
items.prompt: How can Mia help the pond?
items.why: Picking up trash helps keep the pond clean. A clean pond is a healthy home.

items.narration: Which group is found in a healthy place: clean air and water, or smoke and trash?
items.why: Clean air and clean water make a place healthy. Smoke and trash do not.

items.narration: True or false: Dirty air is good for baby birds.
items.prompt: Dirty air is good for birds.
items.why: This is false. Birds need clean air to breathe. Dirty air can make them sick.

items.narration: Which one is a healthy home for a fish: a dry sidewalk, a clean pond, or a dirty puddle?
items.prompt: A healthy home for a fish?
items.why: A clean pond has water and food for fish. A sidewalk has no water.

items.narration: A pond has dirty water. What may happen to the fish: they may get sick, or they grow bigger?
items.why: Dirty water can make fish sick. Fish need clean water to stay well.

items.narration: Which one is the odd one out in a healthy garden: clean soil, clean water, or plastic trash?
items.prompt: Odd one out in a garden
items.why: Plants need clean soil and clean water. Plastic trash does not help them grow.

items.narration: Which one helps keep the air clean: planting trees, or burning trash?
items.why: Trees help keep air clean. Burning trash puts smoke into the air.

items.narration: A clean pond helps a duck meet its needs. Which need can the pond meet: food to eat, a toy, or a phone?
items.prompt: What need does a pond meet?
items.why: A clean pond has plants and bugs for a duck to eat. Toys and phones are not needs.

items.narration: Why should we keep a river clean: because living things need it, or because trash needs a home?
items.why: Fish, birds, and people need clean water. A clean river keeps living things well.

items.narration: Mia has a light toy bucket. What is it made of: plastic or glass?
items.prompt: A toy bucket is made of what?
items.why: A toy bucket is made of plastic. Plastic is light, so it is good for toys.

items.narration: True or false: Wood comes from trees.
items.why: It is true. Wood comes from trees. People cut it to make things like tables and pencils.

items.narration: Which one is made of wood: a pencil, a metal spoon, or a coin?
items.prompt: Which one is made of wood?
items.why: A pencil is made of wood. A metal spoon and a coin are made of metal.

items.narration: Which material can you see through: glass, wood, or metal?
items.why: You can see through glass. Wood and metal block your view.

items.narration: A fork is hard and shiny. What is a fork made of: metal or cloth?
items.prompt: A fork is made of what?
items.why: A fork is made of metal. Metal is hard, shiny, and strong.

items.narration: A hammer has a metal head. What is its handle often made of: wood or glass?
items.prompt: What is a hammer handle often made of?
items.why: Many hammer handles are wood. Glass would break, so it is not used.

items.narration: Which one is the odd one out: a wood spoon, a wood chair, or a metal fork?
items.prompt: Which is the odd one out?
items.why: The wood spoon and wood chair are made of wood. The metal fork is made of metal.

items.narration: Mia has a glass jar. Which group does it go in: made of glass or made of wood?
items.prompt: Which group is the jar in?
items.why: A glass jar is made of glass. It goes with the things made of glass.

items.narration: True or false: Some objects are made of more than one material.
items.prompt: Some things use more than one material.
items.why: It is true. A hammer has a metal head and a wood handle.

items.narration: Which one uses two materials: a glass marble, a wood block, or a wood and metal chair?
items.why: The chair has wood parts and metal parts. The marble and the block use just one material.

items.narration: A bridge must be very strong. Which material is strong enough for a bridge: metal, paper, or cloth?
items.prompt: Which is strong enough for a bridge?
items.why: Metal is strong, so it holds up a bridge. Paper and cloth would bend and tear.

items.narration: Which one is a material, not an object: wood, a chair, or a cup?
items.why: Wood is a material. A chair and a cup are objects made from it.

items.narration: Which one can break into sharp glass pieces if it falls: a glass cup, a metal spoon, or a cloth bag?
items.prompt: Which can break into sharp glass pieces?
items.why: Glass can break into sharp pieces. A metal spoon and a cloth bag do not. If glass breaks, ask a grown-up for help.

items.narration: The playhouse has a wood door, glass window, and metal lock. How many materials: 2 materials, 1 material, 4 materials, or 3 materials?
items.prompt: How many materials are in the playhouse?
items.why: Wood, glass, and metal are 3 different materials. So the playhouse uses 3 materials.

items.narration: True or false: A pencil can have wood and metal parts.
items.prompt: A pencil can have wood and metal.
items.why: It is true. A pencil is wood. Many have a metal band that holds the eraser.

items.narration: Mia sees night. What comes after night: day, or winter?
items.why: After night, the sun comes up and a new day starts. Day and night repeat.

items.narration: True or false: after night, the day comes back again.
items.why: It is true. The sun comes up after every night. Day and night repeat.

items.narration: Which one is a cycle: day and night, or a rock sitting still?
items.why: Day and night happen again and again. A rock sitting still does not repeat.

items.narration: How many seasons are in a year: two, four, or six?
items.why: There are four seasons: spring, summer, fall, and winter. Then they start again.

items.narration: Which season is often cold and snowy: winter, or summer?
items.prompt: Which season is cold and snowy?
items.why: Winter is the cold season with snow. Summer is warm.

items.narration: Which one happens every day: the sun comes up, or the first snowfall?
items.why: The sun comes up every morning. Snow only comes in the cold season.

items.narration: The seasons go spring, summer, fall. What season comes next: winter, spring, or summer?
items.why: Winter comes after fall. Then spring comes back and the cycle starts again.

items.narration: Which is not a cycle: four seasons, day and night, or a cup that breaks?
items.why: Seasons and day and night repeat. A cup breaks once. It does not come back.

items.narration: After winter, what season comes next: spring, fall, or summer?
items.why: Spring comes after winter. The seasons go around and around.

items.narration: True or false: after winter, the seasons stop.
items.why: It is false. After winter, spring comes. The seasons keep repeating.

items.narration: Day, night, day. What comes next: night, or day?
items.why: The pattern goes day, night, day, night. After day, night comes next.

items.narration: Leaves fall off many trees in fall. What season comes just before winter: summer, fall, or spring?
items.why: Fall comes just before winter. The order is spring, summer, fall, winter.

items.narration: In which season do many trees grow new leaves: spring, winter, or fall?
items.prompt: When do trees grow new leaves?
items.why: Many trees grow new leaves in spring. In fall, their leaves drop off.

items.narration: Which happens in the morning: the sun comes up, or the sun goes down?
items.why: The sun comes up in the morning. It goes down at the end of the day.

items.narration: What is a set of events that repeat called: a cycle, a game, or a plant?
items.why: Events that repeat in the same order are called a cycle. Seasons are a cycle.

items.narration: Which animal is bigger: a mouse, or a horse?
items.why: A horse is much bigger than a mouse. Size is one way to compare animals.

items.narration: Which animal has feathers: a fish, a bird, or a dog?
items.why: Birds have feathers. Fish have scales, and dogs have fur.

items.narration: True or false: A kitten gets bigger as it grows. True, or false?
items.why: This is true. Size changes as an animal grows. A kitten becomes a bigger cat.

items.narration: Which animal has fur: a snake, a rabbit, or a frog?
items.why: A rabbit has soft fur. A snake has scales, and a frog has smooth skin.

items.narration: Which is the odd one out: a robin, a sparrow, a cat, or an owl?
items.why: A robin, a sparrow, and an owl are birds with feathers. A cat has fur.

items.narration: A puppy grows into a dog. What stays the same: its size, its four legs, or its weight?
items.why: A puppy and a dog both have four legs. Size and weight change as it grows.

items.narration: A lamb grows into a sheep. What changes: it gets bigger, or it has four legs?
items.why: A lamb gets bigger as it grows. It has four legs the whole time.

items.narration: Which animal has scales for a covering: a rabbit, a duck, or a fish?
items.why: A fish has scales. A rabbit has fur, and a duck has feathers.

items.narration: True or false: A chick's soft fluff stays the same its whole life. True, or false?
items.why: This is false. A chick's fluff changes into feathers as it grows up.

items.narration: Mia sees that a giraffe is tall and a mouse is tiny. What is she comparing: size, covering, or sound?
items.why: Tall and tiny are about how big an animal is. That is size.

items.narration: Which two animals have the same kind of covering: a hen and a duck, a fish and a bear, a frog and a cat, or a snake and a rabbit?
items.why: A hen and a duck are both birds with feathers. The other pairs have different coverings.

items.narration: A kitten grows into a cat. What does not change: its whiskers, its size, or its weight?
items.why: A kitten has whiskers and a cat has whiskers too. Size and weight change as it grows.

items.narration: What comes first as a duckling grows: fluffy down, or adult feathers?
items.why: A duckling starts with fluffy down. Adult feathers grow in later.

items.narration: What is the hard, pointed part on a bird's face called: a fin, a beak, or a tail?
items.why: A bird's hard, pointed mouth is called a beak. Fins are on fish.

items.narration: True or false: Two animals can be the same size but have different coverings. True, or false?
items.why: This is true. A hen and a rabbit can be about the same size. One has feathers and one has fur.

items.narration: A butterfly grows in steps. What is the first stage of a butterfly's life: an egg, a caterpillar, or an adult butterfly?
items.why: A butterfly starts as a tiny egg. The caterpillar hatches from it next.

items.narration: A baby frog lives in water and has a tail. What is it called: a tadpole, a chick, or a caterpillar?
items.prompt: What is a baby frog called?
items.why: A baby frog is a tadpole. A chick is a baby bird. A caterpillar is a baby butterfly.

items.narration: A bird begins its life in one place. Where does a bird begin: in an egg, in a pond, or in a leaf?
items.why: Every bird starts inside an egg. The chick hatches out when it is ready.

items.narration: True or false: a puppy is a baby mammal that drinks its mother's milk.
items.why: A puppy is a mammal. It is born alive and drinks milk from its mother.

items.narration: Some babies drink their mother's milk. Which baby drinks milk: a kitten, a chick, or a tadpole?
items.why: A kitten is a baby mammal, and mammals drink milk. Chicks and tadpoles hatch from eggs.

items.narration: A caterpillar eats and grows. Then it makes a hard shell. What stage is inside the shell: an egg, a pupa, or a tadpole?
items.prompt: What stage is inside the shell?
items.why: After the caterpillar stage comes the pupa. The change into a butterfly happens inside the shell.

items.narration: A tadpole grows back legs and front legs. What stage comes next: an egg, a froglet, or a pupa?
items.why: A tadpole grows legs and becomes a froglet. Later the froglet is an adult frog.

items.narration: A pupa is a stage inside a hard shell. Which animal has a pupa stage in its life: a frog, a robin, or a butterfly?
items.prompt: Which animal has a pupa stage?
items.why: A butterfly is an insect, and it has a pupa stage. Frogs and robins do not.

items.narration: Find the odd one out. Which animal does not hatch from an egg: a robin, a frog, or a horse?
items.prompt: Which is the odd one out?
items.why: A horse is a mammal. It is born alive. Robins and frogs hatch from eggs.

items.narration: A bird's life cycle starts again when eggs are laid. Which stage lays the eggs: an egg, a chick, or an adult bird?
items.why: Only an adult bird can lay eggs. Then new chicks hatch and the cycle starts again.

items.narration: Which is the right order for a bird's life? Is it: egg, chick, adult bird; or chick, egg, adult bird; or adult bird, egg, chick?
items.prompt: Pick the right order for a bird.
items.why: A bird starts as an egg. A chick hatches and grows into an adult bird.

items.narration: A butterfly and a frog have something the same in their life cycles. What is it: They both start as eggs, Both have a pupa, or Both drink milk?
items.why: Butterflies and frogs both start as eggs. A butterfly has a pupa stage, but a frog does not. Mammal babies drink milk.

items.narration: True or false: a kitten hatches from an egg.
items.why: A kitten is a mammal. It is born alive and drinks milk. It does not hatch from an egg.

items.narration: One baby looks like a small adult when it is born. Which one: a puppy, a caterpillar, or a tadpole?
items.prompt: Which baby looks like a small adult?
items.why: A puppy looks like a small dog. A caterpillar and a tadpole look very different from the adults.

items.narration: Mia wants to see the cycle start again. Which stage can lay eggs to begin it: a tadpole, a frog, or a caterpillar?
items.why: Only an adult can lay eggs. A tadpole and a caterpillar are still growing, so the adult frog lays them.

items.narration: Which one is a liquid: a puddle, a rock, or a brick?
items.why: A puddle is water, and water is a liquid. It can flow. Rocks and bricks are solids.

items.narration: Which one is a solid: milk, a chair, or juice?
items.why: A chair keeps its own shape, so it is a solid. Milk and juice are liquids.

items.narration: True or false: a rock is a solid.
items.why: It is true. A rock keeps its own shape, and it does not pour.

items.narration: What can a liquid do: pour, or stay hard?
items.why: A liquid can pour and flow. It takes the shape of its container. A solid keeps its own shape.

items.narration: A brick is used to build walls. Is a brick a liquid or a solid?
items.why: A brick keeps its own shape and does not pour. That makes it a solid.

items.narration: Which one is the odd one out: water, milk, a spoon, or juice?
items.why: Water, milk, and juice are liquids. A spoon is a solid, so it does not belong.

items.narration: Which one in a town is a solid: a brick wall, rain, or a puddle?
items.why: A brick wall keeps its shape, so it is a solid. Rain and puddles are liquid water.

items.narration: Which one in nature is a liquid: a tree, a lake, or a stone?
items.why: A lake is full of water, and water is a liquid. Trees and stones are solids.

items.narration: True or false: a solid keeps its own shape.
items.why: It is true. A solid, like a block or a key, keeps its shape. A liquid does not.

items.narration: Which one is a liquid: a rock, a leaf, or rain?
items.why: Rain is water that falls from the sky. Water is a liquid. A rock and a leaf are solids.

items.narration: Ice sits in the warm sun. What does it become: liquid water, a rock, or a brick?
items.why: Ice is frozen water. When it melts in the warm sun, it turns into liquid water.

items.narration: Mia fills a cup. Which one can she pour into the cup: soup, a toy block, or a stick?
items.why: Soup is a liquid, so it can pour into a cup. A toy block and a stick are solids.

items.narration: Which one is the odd one out: wood, glass, brick, or juice?
items.why: Wood, glass, and brick are solids used to build things. Juice is a liquid, so it is the odd one.

items.narration: A bottle is full of juice. Which part is the liquid: the bottle, the juice, or the cap?
items.why: The juice pours, so it is the liquid. The bottle and the cap keep their shape, so they are solids.

items.narration: True or false: when you pour a liquid into a bowl, it keeps its old shape.
items.why: It is false. A liquid takes the shape of the bowl that holds it. A solid keeps its own shape.

items.narration: What fills a blown-up balloon: air, a rock, or sand?
items.why: We blow air into a balloon. The air takes up space and makes the balloon bigger.

items.narration: True or false? Water flows.
items.why: Water flows. We can pour it from one cup to another.

items.narration: Which one can you pour: water, a rock, or a book?
items.why: Water flows, so you can pour it. A rock and a book stay hard.

items.narration: Moving air is called what: wind, rain, or snow?
items.why: Air that moves is called wind. We can feel it on our face.

items.narration: What do we breathe in: air, water, or sand?
items.why: We breathe in air. Clean air helps living things stay healthy.

items.narration: Mia pours water from a tall glass into a wide bowl. What does the water do: It fits the bowl, It stays tall, or It turns hard?
items.why: Water takes the shape of its container. In a wide bowl, it spreads out to fit.

items.narration: True or false? Air takes up space.
items.why: Air takes up space. That is why a balloon gets bigger when we fill it.

items.narration: Mia blows air into a flat balloon. What happens next: It gets bigger, It gets smaller, or It turns to water?
items.why: Air takes up space. When Mia blows air in, the balloon gets bigger.

items.narration: Which one can we not see: air, a cup, or a book?
items.why: We can't see air. But we can feel it when it moves as wind.

items.narration: Which one does not flow: milk, juice, or a brick?
items.why: Milk and juice flow, so we can pour them. A brick is hard and does not flow.

items.narration: A bottle looks empty. Its lid is on tight. What is inside: air, nothing at all, or sand?
items.prompt: What is in an empty bottle?
items.why: An empty-looking bottle is full of air. Air takes up space even when we can't see it.

items.narration: Mia pours water into a round jar. Then she pours it into a square box. What does the water do: It fits each one, It stays round, or It disappears?
items.why: Water takes the shape of any container. It fits the jar, and then it fits the box.

items.narration: We can't see air. How can we know it is there: A flag waves, A rock sits, or A cup is red?
items.prompt: How can we tell air is there?
items.why: Moving air is wind. When a flag waves, we know air is pushing it.

items.narration: Which is the odd one out: water, milk, juice, or a ball?
items.why: Water, milk, and juice all flow. A ball is solid and does not flow.

items.narration: True or false? Water has its own shape that never changes.
items.why: Water takes the shape of its container. Its shape changes when we pour it somewhere new.

items.narration: What do people breathe in to live: air, rocks, or sand?
items.why: People breathe in air to live. Rocks and sand are not for breathing.

items.narration: Mia's puppy is thirsty. What should he drink: sand, water, or paper?
items.why: Animals drink water when they are thirsty. Sand and paper are not for drinking.

items.narration: True or false: Plants need water to live.
items.why: This is true. Plants drink water through their roots. Without water, they cannot live.

items.narration: Where does a goldfish live: in water, in a tree, or in a shoe?
items.why: A goldfish lives in water. It gets the oxygen it needs from the water.

items.narration: Mia is thirsty. What should she drink: glue, water, or soap?
items.why: People drink water to stay healthy. Glue and soap are not safe to drink.

items.narration: What do plant leaves take in from the outside: air, juice, or sand?
items.why: Plant leaves take in air. Plants need air as well as water.

items.narration: Which part of a plant drinks water from the soil: the roots, the petals, or the fruit?
items.why: Roots grow in the soil. They drink water and send it up the plant.

items.narration: Which one breathes air with lungs: a whale, a goldfish, or a clam?
items.why: A whale has lungs. It comes up to the top of the water to breathe air.

items.narration: True or false: A fish gets the oxygen it needs from the water.
items.why: This is true. A fish takes in oxygen from the water with its gills.

items.narration: Mia forgets to water her plant for many days. What happens: it droops and dries out, it grows taller fast, or it turns into a rock?
items.why: Plants need water to live. Without it, they droop and dry out.

items.narration: Which one does not need air and water to live: a tree, a rock, or a cat?
items.why: A rock is not alive. Trees and cats are living things, so they need air and water.

items.narration: Mia pours water on the soil. What does the plant do next: its roots take in water, its leaves fall off, or it starts to sing?
items.why: After Mia waters the soil, the roots take in the water. Then the plant can use it.

items.narration: Which is a way people use water to live: drinking it, breathing it in, or wearing it?
items.why: People drink water to stay healthy. We breathe in air, not water.

items.narration: Which group needs air and water to live: only animals, only plants, or all living things?
items.why: Plants, animals, and people are all living things. All of them need air and water.

items.narration: True or false: A goldfish can live out of water for many days.
items.why: This is false. A fish gets oxygen from water with its gills. It cannot live long without water.

items.narration: Which one does a plant need to grow: water, a toy, or a hat?
items.why: Plants need water to grow. Roots take it in from the soil. A toy or a hat does nothing for a plant.

items.narration: Outside, plants get light and heat from something in the sky. Is it the sun, a shoe, or a spoon?
items.why: The sun gives plants light and heat. Plants use the light to make their food.

items.narration: True or false: plants need air. Is that true, or false?
items.prompt: True or false: plants need air.
items.why: This is true. Plants take in air through their leaves and use it to make food.

items.narration: Maya forgot to water her bean plant for two weeks. What will happen to it: it will wilt, or it will grow fast?
items.why: Without water, a plant droops and wilts. Water helps it stand tall and grow.

items.narration: Which one is not something plants need: air, light, a phone, or water?
items.why: Plants need air, light, and water. A phone is not a need for plants.

items.narration: Soil gives plants water and one more thing. Is it nutrients, music, or toys?
items.why: Soil holds nutrients, which are minerals plants need to grow strong. Roots take them in with water.

items.narration: The sun gives plants two of the things they need. Which two: light and heat, music and toys, or a shoe and a spoon?
items.why: The sun gives plants light and heat. Music, toys, shoes, and spoons are not what plants need.

items.narration: Ben's bean plants are packed so close that their leaves touch. What would help them most: more space, a dark closet, or less water?
items.why: Plants need space for roots and leaves to spread out. Moving some apart gives each plant room.

items.narration: True or false: a plant kept in a dark closet for weeks stays healthy. Is that true, or false?
items.prompt: True or false: no light is fine.
items.why: This is false. Plants need light to make food. In the dark, a plant turns pale and weak.

items.narration: Which one can hurt a tomato plant: a freezing cold night, a sunny window, or a drink of water?
items.why: A freezing night can kill a tomato plant. Plants need heat. Sun and water help them grow.

items.narration: Sam's plant grows in plain sand. Its leaves turn pale and it grows slowly. What is it most likely missing: nutrients, snow, or a cage?
items.why: Plain sand has very few nutrients. Plants need nutrients to grow strong and green.

items.narration: A pot has no holes, so water stays in the soil for weeks. What could happen to the plant: the roots get harmed, it gets more light, or it gets more heat?
items.why: Too much water can harm roots. Roots need air too, and soaked soil leaves little room for it.

items.narration: Which one would not hurt a plant: a long dry spell, a hard frost, a sunny watered spot, or a crowded pot?
items.why: A sunny spot with water gives a plant what it needs. A dry spell, a hard frost, and a crowded pot can all hurt it.

items.narration: A small tree grows in the shade of tall trees in a forest. Which need is hard for it to get: light, music, or sand?
items.prompt: What is hard to get in shade?
items.why: Tall trees block the sun, so a small tree in their shade gets less light. Plants need light to make food.

items.narration: Lena's plant sits in a dark corner. It looks weak and leans toward the room. What helps most: move it to a window, cover it with a box, or take away its water?
items.prompt: A weak plant in a dark corner
items.why: The plant needs light. Moving it to a window gives it light. A box makes it darker, and it still needs water.

items.narration: Which part of a plant holds it in the soil: the roots, the flower, or the cone?
items.prompt: What holds the plant in the soil?
items.why: Roots grow down into the soil. They hold the plant in place and take in water.

items.narration: Which part of a plant uses sunlight to make food: the root, the leaf, or the seed?
items.why: Leaves use sunlight, air, and water to make food for the plant.

items.narration: Mia plants a seed in a pot and gives it water and light. What can the seed grow into: a stone, a new plant, or a toy?
items.prompt: What can a seed grow into?
items.why: A seed holds a tiny new plant. With water and light, it can grow into a plant.

items.narration: True or false: Roots usually grow down in the soil.
items.prompt: True or false: roots grow in soil.
items.why: That is true. Roots grow down into the soil, where they find water.

items.narration: A pine tree grows its seeds inside a special part. Is it a cone, a root, or a stem?
items.why: Pine trees make seeds inside cones. They do not have flowers or fruit.

items.narration: Which part carries water from the roots up to the leaves: the stem, the flower, or the seed?
items.why: The stem works like a straw. It carries water from the roots up to the leaves.

items.narration: Inside a flower, the stamen makes a yellow dust. What is that dust called: water, pollen, or fruit?
items.why: The stamen makes pollen. Pollen must reach the pistil so seeds can form.

items.narration: The middle part of a flower is where seeds begin to form. What is its name: the pistil, the stamen, or the root?
items.prompt: Name the part where seeds begin.
items.why: The pistil is in the middle of the flower. Seeds begin to form there after pollen arrives.

items.narration: Which one is not a part of a plant: a root, a seed, a cone, or a pebble?
items.prompt: Which is not a plant part?
items.why: Roots, seeds, and cones are all plant parts. A pebble is a small stone, not a part of a plant.

items.narration: An apple tree grows apples. What does the fruit do for the plant: it makes pollen, it drinks water, or it protects the seeds?
items.prompt: What does fruit do for a plant?
items.why: Fruit holds and protects the seeds inside it. Roots drink water, and stamens make pollen.

items.narration: A big wind blows through the park. Why do roots help a tree stay up: they hold it in the soil, they make pollen, or they make seeds?
items.prompt: How do roots help in the wind?
items.why: Roots spread out in the soil and hold the plant in place. Wind does not easily knock it over.

choices.text: they hold it in the soil

items.narration: Mia plants a bean seed. What happens first as it starts to grow: roots grow down, a flower opens, or fruit forms?
items.why: A seed sprouts roots first. They take in water. Flowers and fruit come much later.

items.narration: A tomato plant loses all its leaves. Its roots are fine. Which job does the plant now struggle to do: making food from light, holding itself in soil, or taking in water by roots?
items.prompt: What if a plant loses its leaves?
items.why: Leaves make the plant's food from sunlight, air, and water. Roots still hold the plant and take in water.

items.narration: For seeds to form, pollen from the stamen must land on another flower part. Which part is it: the pistil, the root, or the leaf?
items.why: Pollen from the stamen lands on the pistil. Then seeds can begin to form.

items.narration: Mia eats an asparagus spear for dinner. It is a young shoot of the plant. Which plant part is it: a stem, a root, or a seed?
items.why: An asparagus spear is a young stem. Stems hold plants up and carry water.

items.narration: Which happens first in a life: being a baby, or being in Grade 1?
items.why: Everyone starts as a baby. Grade 1 comes much later, when a child is about 6.

items.narration: Sam learned to walk. Sam also started Kindergarten. Which did Sam do first: learned to walk, or started Kindergarten?
items.why: Children learn to walk when they are very little. Kindergarten comes later.

items.narration: True or false: A baby learns to walk before learning to ride a bike.
items.why: That is true. Walking comes first. Riding a bike comes later, when a child is bigger.

items.narration: Which word means the very start of the line: first, or last?
items.why: First means the very start. Last means the end.

items.narration: Which one is a big life event: learning to walk, a pencil, or a cloud?
items.why: Learning to walk is something that happens in a life. A pencil and a cloud are things, not events.

items.narration: Sam went to daycare, then Kindergarten, then Grade 1. Which came after Kindergarten: daycare, or Grade 1?
items.why: Sam went to daycare first. Kindergarten came next. Grade 1 came after that.

items.narration: Mia rode a tricycle when she was small. Later, she learned to ride a bicycle. What did Mia ride later: a tricycle, or a bicycle?
items.why: The tricycle came first, when Mia was small. The bicycle came later.

items.narration: Ali first crawled. Next, Ali stood up. Then Ali walked. What did Ali do right after standing up: crawled, stood up, or walked?
items.why: The order was crawled, stood up, then walked. Walking came right after standing up.

items.narration: Which word helps us put things in order: first, apple, or blue?
items.why: First, next, then, and last help us put events in order. Apple and blue do not.

items.narration: True or false: Grade 1 happens before Kindergarten.
items.why: That is false. Kindergarten comes first. Then children go to Grade 1.

items.narration: Sam learned to walk, then went to Kindergarten, then started Grade 1. What came between walking and Grade 1: Kindergarten, being a baby, or Grade 2?
items.why: The order was walking, Kindergarten, then Grade 1. Kindergarten is in the middle.

items.narration: Jo is in Grade 1 now. Which already happened for Jo: Kindergarten, Grade 3, or Grade 5?
items.why: Jo finished Kindergarten before Grade 1. Grade 3 and Grade 5 are still to come.

items.narration: Zoe is in Grade 1. Which will happen next in school for Zoe: Grade 2, Kindergarten, or daycare?
items.why: After Grade 1 comes Grade 2. Daycare and Kindergarten came before.

items.narration: Which one is not a big life event: learning to walk, starting Grade 1, or eating lunch today?
items.prompt: Which is the odd one out?
items.why: Walking and starting Grade 1 are big events. Eating lunch happens every day.

items.narration: Ben learned to ride a bike. Then he started Grade 1. Which happened last: learned to ride a bike, or started Grade 1?
items.why: Ben learned to ride a bike first. Then he started Grade 1. Grade 1 is the last one.

items.narration: Which one is natural: a river, a school, or a road?
items.why: A river is natural. Nature made it. A school and a road are built by people.

items.narration: Here is a road. Is a road natural or built?
items.why: People make roads. A road is a built feature.

items.narration: True or false: A forest is a natural feature.
items.why: It is true. Trees in a forest grow by themselves, so a forest is natural.

items.narration: Which one is built by people: a lake, a store, or a hill?
items.why: People built the store. A lake and a hill are natural.

items.narration: Who makes a built feature: people, or nature?
items.why: People make built features, like houses and schools. Nature makes natural ones.

items.narration: Which is the odd one out: a lake, a river, or a library?
items.why: A lake and a river are natural. A library is built, so it is the odd one out.

items.narration: Which group is all built: school, road, house; or river, forest, school?
items.why: A school, a road, and a house are all built. A river and a forest are natural.

items.narration: True or false: A library is a natural feature.
items.why: It is false. People built the library. It is a built feature.

items.narration: Mia wants to borrow a book. Where can she go: a library, a forest, or a lake?
items.prompt: Where can Mia get a book?
items.why: A library is a built place with books to borrow. Forests and lakes are natural.

items.narration: A place of worship is where people gather to pray. Is it natural or built?
items.why: People build places of worship. It is a built feature.

items.narration: Which is the odd one out: a house, an apartment building, a forest, or a school?
items.why: A house, an apartment building, and a school are built. A forest is natural.

items.narration: People made a place for hockey games. Which one is it: an arena, a forest, or a lake?
items.why: People built the arena for sports. A forest and a lake are natural.

items.narration: True or false: Every feature in a community is built by people.
items.why: It is false. Communities have natural features too, like rivers, lakes, and forests.

items.narration: Why is a forest natural? Is it because trees grow by themselves, or because a builder made it?
items.why: Trees grow by themselves. Nature made the forest, not a builder.

items.narration: Which group is all natural: lake, river, forest; or road, lake, forest?
items.why: A lake, a river, and a forest are all natural. A road is built by people.

items.narration: What does a timeline do: puts events in order, makes a snack, or paints a wall?
items.why: A timeline puts events in order. It shows what happened first and what happened last.

items.narration: Grandma, Mom, and baby Sam are in a family. Who is the oldest: Grandma, Mom, or baby Sam?
items.why: Grandma was born the longest time ago. So she is the oldest and goes first.

items.narration: Which word helps put events in order: first, purple, or loud?
items.why: The word first tells us what happened at the start. Words like next and last help too.

items.narration: What does newest mean: happened most recently, or happened long ago?
items.why: Newest means it happened most recently. It goes last on a timeline.

items.narration: True or false: The oldest event goes first on a timeline.
items.why: That is true. A timeline goes from oldest to newest, so the oldest event is first.

items.narration: Dad's life has three events. Which happened first: Dad was born, Dad started Grade 1, or Dad got his first job?
items.why: Dad had to be born before anything else. So being born is the first event.

items.narration: Nana was born first. Then her son Raj was born. Then Raj's daughter Priya was born. Who was born right after Nana: Raj or Priya?
items.prompt: Who was born right after Nana?
items.why: Raj was born next, right after Nana. Priya was born last.

items.narration: Lin's family lived in Winnipeg first. Next they moved to Regina. Last they moved to Calgary. Which was their second home: Winnipeg, Regina, or Calgary?
items.why: Winnipeg was first. Regina came next, so it was the second home. Calgary was last.

items.narration: Which does not belong on a family timeline: a baby was born, we moved to a new town, or my shoe is blue?
items.why: A birth and a move are family events. A blue shoe is not an event, so it does not belong.

choices.text: we moved to a new town

items.narration: Mia's mom was born before Mia. True or false: Mia goes before her mom on the timeline.
items.prompt: Does Mia go before her mom?
items.why: That is false. Mom was born first, so she goes first. Mia was born later, so she goes after.

items.narration: Omar's grandpa moved to Canada. Then Omar's dad was born. Then Omar was born. Which came between the move and Omar's birth: Dad was born, Omar started school, or Grandpa was born?
items.why: Dad was born after the move and before Omar. Omar's school came later. Grandpa was born before the move.

items.narration: Grandma was born. Then Mom was born. Then Mom had baby Sam. Which event goes last on the timeline: Grandma was born, Mom was born, or Mom had baby Sam?
items.why: Baby Sam is the newest person. Mom having Sam happened last, so it goes at the end.

items.narration: A family has a spring picnic, a summer camp, and a fall harvest feast. Which comes right after the summer camp: the spring picnic or the fall harvest feast?
items.why: The seasons go spring, summer, fall, winter. Fall comes right after summer, so the harvest feast is next.

items.narration: Grandparents, parents, and children are three generations. Which generation was born most recently: the grandparents, the parents, or the children?
items.why: Children are born after their parents. Parents are born after the grandparents. So the children are the newest.

items.narration: Jo moved three times. Barrie at age 3. Ottawa at age 9. Kingston at age 6. Which move was last: Barrie, Ottawa, or Kingston?
items.why: Jo was oldest, age 9, for the Ottawa move. A bigger age means it happened later. So Ottawa was last.

items.narration: Maya is hungry. Why do our bodies need food: for energy, or to feel bored?
items.why: Food gives our bodies energy. Energy helps us run, play, and learn.

items.narration: True or false: Food helps our bodies grow.
items.why: That is true. Food helps your bones, muscles, skin, and teeth grow.

items.narration: What gives your body energy to run and play: food, a toy, or a blanket?
items.why: Food gives your body energy. A toy or a blanket cannot do that.

items.narration: Which part of you helps you think and learn: your brain, your knee, or your nose?
items.why: Your brain helps you think and learn. Food helps your brain grow and work well.

items.narration: Milk helps your bones grow strong. What else do our bodies get from food: energy, or a loud noise?
items.prompt: What do we get from food?
items.why: Food gives us energy. It does not make noise.

items.narration: Sam feels tired, and his tummy is empty. What can he do to get energy: eat a snack, or look at clouds?
items.why: Food gives us energy. A healthy snack can help Sam feel better.

items.narration: Which is a reason we eat food: to help our bones grow, or to make our shoes fit?
items.why: Food helps our bones grow strong. Shoes are not changed by what we eat.

items.narration: Which one does food NOT give us: energy, strong muscles, or a new bike?
items.why: Food gives us energy and strong muscles. It cannot give us a new bike.

items.narration: Food helps the part of you that covers your body stay healthy. Is it your skin, a shoe, or a hat?
items.why: Your skin covers your body. Food helps your skin stay healthy.

items.narration: True or false: Only our muscles need food.
items.why: That is false. Our teeth, skin, bones, muscles, and brain all need food.

items.narration: Leo did not eat lunch. Now he feels weak and cannot think well. Why: his body needs energy, or it is too sunny?
items.why: Our bodies need food for energy. Without it, we can feel weak and find it hard to think.

items.narration: Sometimes a child is often hungry and has no food. Who can help: a trusted adult, or no one?
items.prompt: Who can help if you are hungry?
items.why: A trusted adult can help you get food. A parent or teacher is one. It is okay to ask.

items.narration: Muscles help you move. Eggs and beans help muscles grow. What do muscles help you do: move, or hear?
items.why: Muscles help you move, like when you run or jump. Food helps them grow strong.

items.narration: Our bodies use energy even when we sit still. Do we need food when we rest: body still needs energy, or only when we run?
items.why: Your body works all day, even when you rest. It always needs energy from food.

items.narration: Mia has a big race today. What should she do first to have energy: eat a healthy meal, or skip her meal?
items.why: Eating a healthy meal gives Mia energy for her race. Skipping food would leave her tired.

items.narration: Which drink should be your first choice: water, pop, or fruit punch?
items.why: Canada's Food Guide tells us to make water our first choice. Water is good for our bodies.

items.narration: A carrot is a food. Which group does a carrot belong to: vegetables and fruits, protein foods, or whole grain foods?
items.prompt: Which group is a carrot in?
items.why: A carrot is a vegetable. It goes in the vegetables and fruits group.

items.narration: True or false: half of your plate should be vegetables and fruits.
items.prompt: Half the plate is vegetables and fruits.
items.why: That is true. The biggest part of the plate is vegetables and fruits.

items.narration: Which food is a protein food: eggs, a peach, or oatmeal?
items.why: Eggs are a protein food. A peach is a fruit, and oatmeal is a whole grain food.

items.narration: Which food is the odd one out: apple, pear, or bread?
items.prompt: Which is the odd one out?
items.why: Apples and pears are fruits. Bread is not a fruit.

items.narration: Which food is a whole grain food: oatmeal, broccoli, or tofu?
items.prompt: Which is a whole grain food?
items.why: Oatmeal is made from a whole grain. Broccoli is a vegetable, and tofu is a protein food.

items.narration: How much of the plate is for whole grain foods: one quarter, half, or none?
items.prompt: How much is whole grain foods?
items.why: Whole grain foods fill one quarter of the plate. Vegetables and fruits fill half.

items.narration: Sam has a plate with only rice. What could he add: carrots and peas, candy, or chips?
items.why: Carrots and peas are vegetables. Adding them helps fill half the plate with vegetables and fruits.

items.narration: What helps us eat well: eating many kinds of food, or eating only one food?
items.why: Different foods give our bodies different good things. Eating many kinds helps us eat well.

items.narration: True or false: fish is a protein food.
items.why: That is true. Fish, beans, eggs, and tofu are all protein foods.

items.narration: Beans, eggs, tofu, and spinach. Which one is the odd one out: beans, eggs, tofu, or spinach?
items.prompt: Which is the odd one out?
items.why: Beans, eggs, and tofu are protein foods. Spinach is a vegetable, so it is the odd one out.

items.narration: Which plate is best for eating well: peas, brown rice, fish; cookies and candy; or chips and pop?
items.why: Peas are vegetables. Brown rice is a whole grain. Fish is a protein food. That is a good plate.

items.narration: Sam's plate is half vegetables and fruits. What goes on the other half: whole grain and protein, candy and pop, or nothing?
items.why: The other half has whole grain foods and protein foods. Together they help us grow strong.

items.narration: True or false: Canada's Food Guide tells us to eat only protein foods.
items.why: That is false. The guide shows many kinds of food on one plate.

items.narration: Mia has whole grain bread and eggs for lunch. What could she add to eat well: carrot sticks, a cookie, or a soda?
items.why: Whole grain bread is a whole grain food and eggs are protein. Carrot sticks add vegetables to finish the plate.
